accepted_answer:
Hello @Zhoros, 
when you return directly an instance of `Response `, in your case `PlainTextResponse`, this is the one that will be used and the one declared in dependecy will be ignored. 
To look at it from another perspective: if a `Response` is declared as a dependency, it will be used to construct the final response together with the value returned by the endpoint. If, instead, an instance of Response is returned directly, that will be taken as the final response.

Hope this helps.

title: Router-tree lazy rebuild (0.137.0+) is not thread-safe: valid routes can 404 under concurrent first requests
question_body:
### First Check

- [X] I added a very descriptive title here.
- [X] I used the GitHub search to find a similar question and didn't find it.
- [X] I searched the FastAPI documentation, with the integrated search.
- [X] I already searched in Google "How to X in FastAPI" and didn't find any information.
- [X] I already read and followed all the tutorial in the docs and didn't find an answer.
- [X] I already checked if it is not related to FastAPI but to [Pydantic](https://github.com/pydantic/pydantic).
- [X] I already checked if it is not related to FastAPI but to [Swagger UI](https://github.com/swagger-api/swagger-ui).
- [X] I already checked if it is not related to FastAPI but to [ReDoc](https://github.com/Redocly/redoc).

### Commit to Help

- [X] I commit to help with one of those options 👆

### Example Code

```python
"""Pure public API: N threads issue the app's FIRST requests concurrently,
each through its own TestClient (own event loop per thread). All requests
return 200 here, but the interleaved unlocked rebuilds leave the included
router's cached candidate list with far more than len(routes) entries —
permanently — and corrupt the global warnings filters. The same unlocked
window can also 404 valid routes (deterministic script in the description).
"""
import threading
import warnings

import fastapi
from fastapi import APIRouter, FastAPI
from starlette.testclient import TestClient

N_ROUTES = 120
N_THREADS = 6


def build_app() -> FastAPI:
    app = FastAPI()
    router = APIRouter()
    for i in range(N_ROUTES):
        def endpoint(q: int = 0, _i: int = i):
            return {"i": _i, "q": q}

        router.add_api_route(f"/r{i}", endpoint, methods=["GET"])
    app.include_router(router)
    return app


def main() -> int:
    print(f"fastapi {fastapi.__version__}")
    filters_before = len(warnings.filters)

    app = build_app()
    barrier = threading.Barrier(N_THREADS)
    statuses = []

    def worker() -> None:
        client = TestClient(app)
        barrier.wait()
        statuses.append(client.get(f"/r{N_ROUTES - 1}").status_code)

    threads = [threading.Thread(target=worker) for _ in range(N_THREADS)]
    for t in threads:
        t.start()
    for t in threads:
        t.join()

    from fastapi.routing import _IncludedRouter

    included = next(r for r in app.router.routes if isinstance(r, _IncludedRouter))
    cache_len = len(included._effective_candidates)
    print(f"statuses: {statuses}")
    print(f"cached candidates: {cache_len} (expected {N_ROUTES})")
    if len(warnings.filters) != filters_before:
        print(f"warnings.filters leaked: {filters_before} -> {len(warnings.filters)}")
    return 1 if cache_len != N_ROUTES else 0


if __name__ == "__main__":
    import sys

    sys.exit(main())
```


### Description

Since the router-inclusion refactor in 0.137.0 (#15745), `_IncludedRouter.effective_candidates()` and `effective_low_priority_routes()` (`fastapi/routing.py`) rebuild their cached candidate lists lazily on first request with no synchronization:

```python
routes_version = self.original_router._get_routes_version()
if routes_version == self._effective_candidates_version:   # (1) check
    return self._effective_candidates
self._effective_candidates = []                            # (2) wipe: publishes an EMPTY list on the shared attribute
...                                                        # (3) incremental self._effective_candidates.append(...)
self._effective_candidates_version = routes_version        # (4) stamp
```

(`fastapi/routing.py:1583-1602` in 0.139.0; identical on current `master`.)

When more than one thread drives the same app object — e.g. a test suite whose worker threads each own a `TestClient` against one shared app, or any multi-loop/threaded embedding — the app's first concurrent requests race this rebuild. Three observable failures:

**1. Spurious 404 on a valid route.** A thread preempted between (1) and (2) that resumes after another thread completed (4) wipes a version-stamped cache. Until the wiper's own rebuild re-appends the tail routes, every request passes the check (1), iterates a half-built list, gets `Match.NONE`, and falls through to `Router.default` (`await self.default(scope, receive, send)`, `routing.py:2730`) → bare `404 {'detail': 'Not Found'}` for a perfectly valid path/method. We first noticed exactly this as intermittent 404s on an app's first requests in a real project's test suite (per-thread `TestClient`s against one shared app).

**2. Permanent candidate-cache corruption — the Example Code above; reproduces essentially every run.** Concurrent rebuilds interleave their `append`s into the same last-assigned list, so the cache ends up with up to `N_threads x N_routes` entries. Typical output:

```
fastapi 0.139.0
statuses: [200, 200, 200, 200, 200, 200]
cached candidates: 283 (expected 120)
warnings.filters leaked: 5 -> 6
```

(Observed 5/5 runs corrupted, counts varying with interleaving: 283, 166, 226, 247, 375.) Every subsequent request then iterates the duplicated candidates for the lifetime of the app.

**3. Global warnings-filter corruption.** The rebuild constructs pydantic `TypeAdapter`s per route inside `warnings.catch_warnings()` (`fastapi/_compat/v2.py`, `ModelField.__post_init__`). `catch_warnings` mutates process-global state, so concurrent enter/exit corrupts `warnings.filters` — leaked filter entries (see output above) and `UnsupportedFieldAttributeWarning` escaping to stderr.

### Deterministic reproduction of the 404

The 404 needs a specific preemption: between (1) and (2), across another thread's (4). This script forces exactly that schedule by pausing the first rebuilder at two *legal* preemption points with a `threading.settrace` hook — FastAPI code and behavior are untouched; the hook only makes an OS-schedulable interleaving reproducible. Three requests to the same valid route:

<details>
<summary>repro_404_deterministic.py</summary>

```python
import inspect
import sys
import threading

import fastapi
import fastapi.routing as fastapi_routing
from fastapi import APIRouter, FastAPI
from starlette.testclient import TestClient

N_ROUTES = 120


def build_app() -> FastAPI:
    app = FastAPI()
    router = APIRouter()
    for i in range(N_ROUTES):
        def endpoint(q: int = 0, _i: int = i):
            return {"i": _i, "q": q}

        router.add_api_route(f"/r{i}", endpoint, methods=["GET"])
    app.include_router(router)
    return app


def find_lines() -> tuple:
    func = fastapi_routing._IncludedRouter.effective_candidates
    lines, start = inspect.getsourcelines(func)
    wipe = append = None
    for i, line in enumerate(lines):
        if "_effective_candidates = []" in line:
            wipe = start + i
        if "_effective_candidates.append(route_context)" in line:
            append = start + i
    if wipe is None or append is None:
        raise AssertionError("lines not found - fastapi internals changed?")
    return func.__code__, wipe, append


CODE, WIPE_LINE, APPEND_LINE = find_lines()
victim_parked = threading.Event()       # victim sits between check (1) and wipe (2)
victim_release = threading.Event()
victim_mid_rebuild = threading.Event()  # victim wiped + appended <=1 entry
victim_finish = threading.Event()
_parked_once = False
_parked_mid = False
_victim_ident = None


def install_schedule_points() -> None:
    """Two legal preemption points for the FIRST thread that rebuilds (the
    'victim'; both apply to that same thread only). The ASGI app runs on anyio
    portal threads spawned by each TestClient, so we key on 'first arriver'."""

    def local_trace(frame, event, arg):
        global _parked_once, _parked_mid, _victim_ident
        if event == "line":
            if frame.f_lineno == WIPE_LINE and not _parked_once:
                _parked_once = True
                _victim_ident = threading.get_ident()
                victim_parked.set()
                victim_release.wait()   # P1: parked exactly between (1) and (2)
            elif (
                frame.f_lineno == APPEND_LINE
                and threading.get_ident() == _victim_ident
                and not _parked_mid
            ):
                _parked_mid = True
                victim_mid_rebuild.set()
                victim_finish.wait()    # P2: wiped, list nearly empty
        return local_trace

    def global_trace(frame, event, arg):
        if frame.f_code is CODE:
            return local_trace
        return None

    threading.settrace(global_trace)


def main() -> int:
    print(f"fastapi {fastapi.__version__}, python {sys.version.split()[0]}")
    app = build_app()
    target = f"/r{N_ROUTES - 1}"  # a perfectly valid route
    statuses = {}

    install_schedule_points()

    def request(name: str) -> None:
        client = TestClient(app)  # own event loop per thread
        r = client.get(target)
        statuses[name] = (r.status_code, r.json())

    victim = threading.Thread(target=request, args=("victim",), name="victim")
    victim.start()
    assert victim_parked.wait(timeout=30), "victim never reached the wipe line"

    # While the victim sits between (1) and (2): a normal request fully
    # builds the cache and stamps the version.
    warmer = threading.Thread(target=request, args=("warmer",), name="warmer")
    warmer.start()
    warmer.join()
    included = next(
        r for r in app.router.routes
        if isinstance(r, fastapi_routing._IncludedRouter)
    )
    assert statuses["warmer"][0] == 200, statuses["warmer"]
    assert included._effective_candidates_version is not None, "cache not stamped"
    assert len(included._effective_candidates) == N_ROUTES

    # Release the victim: its very next bytecode wipes the stamped cache.
    # It is paused again (P2) right at the first append of its rebuild loop.
    victim_release.set()
    assert victim_mid_rebuild.wait(timeout=30), "victim never reached the append line"
    assert len(included._effective_candidates) <= 1, "wipe did not land as scheduled"
    assert included._effective_candidates_version is not None  # version still stamped!

    # A third, completely ordinary request: version check passes, list is
    # half-built -> falls through to Router.default -> 404.
    reader = threading.Thread(target=request, args=("reader",), name="reader")
    reader.start()
    reader.join()

    victim_finish.set()
    victim.join()

    for name in ("warmer", "victim", "reader"):
        print(f"{name:>7}: {statuses[name]}")

    ok = (
        statuses["warmer"][0] == 200
        and statuses["victim"][0] == 200
        and statuses["reader"][0] == 404
    )
    if ok:
        print(f"\nBUG REPRODUCED: valid route {target} returned 404 after the "
              "version-stamped candidate cache was wiped by a concurrently "
              "rebuilding thread.")
        return 1
    print("\nschedule did not produce the 404 (unexpected)")
    return 0


if __name__ == "__main__":
    sys.exit(main())
```

</details>

Output (identical on a pristine `pip install fastapi httpx` venv):

```
fastapi 0.139.0, python 3.12.13
 warmer: (200, {'i': 119, 'q': 0})
 victim: (200, {'i': 119, 'q': 0})
 reader: (404, {'detail': 'Not Found'})

BUG REPRODUCED: valid route /r119 returned 404 after the version-stamped
candidate cache was wiped by a concurrently rebuilding thread.
```

Under plain concurrent load the same window is hit stochastically (CPU load increases the rate); the Example Code shows the underlying interleaving happens essentially every time, so hitting the 404 in the wild is a matter of scheduling luck, not of whether the race exists.

### Who is exposed

A single-event-loop server (typical uvicorn worker) matches routes on one thread, so it does not contend on the rebuild. Exposed are setups where one app object is driven from multiple threads/loops: parallel test suites with per-thread `TestClient`s, threaded/multi-loop embeddings, apps shared across loops.

### Suggested fix

Build into a local list and publish only when complete, stamping after publishing; concurrent rebuilds then become redundant but harmless:

```python
def effective_candidates(self):
    routes_version = self.original_router._get_routes_version()
    if routes_version == self._effective_candidates_version:
        return self._effective_candidates
    candidates: list[_EffectiveRouteContext | _IncludedRouter] = []
    for route in self.original_router.routes:
        ...  # append to the local `candidates`
    self._effective_candidates = candidates
    self._effective_candidates_version = routes_version
    return candidates
```

Same pattern for `effective_low_priority_routes()`. A `threading.Lock` would also close the window and additionally serialize the redundant rebuild work; the local-build variant relies on CPython attribute-store atomicity, so free-threaded builds may still want the lock. Note that the `warnings.catch_warnings()` usage in `ModelField.__post_init__` stays inherently thread-unsafe whenever model fields are built at request time — even with the rebuild race fixed, two loops building adapters concurrently can still corrupt the global filters; that may deserve a separate look.

### Affected versions

Introduced with the router-tree refactor #15745 in **0.137.0** (verified: 0.136.0 has no `_IncludedRouter`; 0.137.0 has the identical unlocked pattern). Reproduced on **0.139.0** (current latest); the code is unchanged on current `master`. Also relevant: starlette 1.3.1, httpx 0.28.1, anyio 4.14.1.

### Operating System

macOS

### Operating System Details

macOS 26.5.1 (arm64, Apple Silicon)

### FastAPI Version

0.139.0

### Pydantic Version

2.13.4

### Python Version

3.12.13

### Additional Context

starlette 1.3.1, httpx 0.28.1, anyio 4.14.1 (reproduced both in a project venv and in a pristine `pip install fastapi httpx` venv). Verified the same unlocked pattern in the 0.137.0 and 0.138.0 wheels and on current master; 0.136.0 predates `_IncludedRouter`. Searched issues, PRs and discussions for `effective_candidates`, `_IncludedRouter`, router thread safety and concurrent-404 reports before posting - no existing report found.
accepted_answer:
This is quite an interesting edge case! Thanks for the report.

It should solved here: https://github.com/fastapi/fastapi/pull/16013

The issue should be mostly harmless, as it would mainly apply in threaded parallel test runs (rare). But still, I thought it would be worth solving.

For the warnings, it's also pretty much harmless and that will be refactored either way so it should be fine. It is now released as 0.139.2 :tada:

title: Why does uploading a large file (over 2MB) cause subsequent requests to retrieve the pre-reset ContextVar within a short time frame (1-2 seconds)?

### Example Code

```python
import threading
import time
from contextvars import ContextVar
from typing import Optional

import httpx
import uvicorn
from fastapi import FastAPI, UploadFile

CTX: ContextVar[Optional[str]] = ContextVar('TEST_FILE_UPLOAD', default=None)


class GatewayMiddleware:
    def __init__(self, app) -> None:
        self.app = app

    async def __call__(self, scope, receive, send) -> None:
        now = str(time.time())
        print(f'{now} url->{scope.get("path")}')

        old_ctx_val = CTX.get()
        assert old_ctx_val is None, f'Must be None! old_ctx_val: {old_ctx_val}'

        ctx_val = now
        print(f'{now} ctx_val->{ctx_val}')
        token = CTX.set(ctx_val)

        await self.app(scope, receive, send)

        CTX.reset(token)
        new_ctx_val = CTX.get()
        assert new_ctx_val is None, f'Must be None! new_ctx_val: {new_ctx_val}'


def test_server() -> None:
    app = FastAPI()
    app.add_middleware(GatewayMiddleware)

    @app.post('/test')
    @app.get('/test')
    async def test():
        return 'test'

    @app.post('/upload')
    async def upload(file: UploadFile):
        await file.close()
        return 'upload2'

    uvicorn.run(app, host="0.0.0.0", port=8010)


def test_client() -> None:
    print('\nTest 1: Small file processing... Expected to succeed')
    with httpx.Client() as client:
        client.post('http://127.0.0.1:8010/upload', files={'file': b'\x00' * (1 * 1024 * 1024)})
        # success
        client.post('http://127.0.0.1:8010/test')
    print('\nTest 2: Large file processing with short intervals... Typically fails')
    with httpx.Client() as client:
        client.post('http://127.0.0.1:8010/upload', files={'file': b'\x00' * (2 * 1024 * 1024)})
        time.sleep(1)
        # error!
        client.post('http://127.0.0.1:8010/test')
    print('\nTest 3: Large file processing with long intervals... Expected to succeed')
    with httpx.Client() as client:
        client.post('http://127.0.0.1:8010/upload', files={'file': b'\x00' * (2 * 1024 * 1024)})
        time.sleep(10)
        # success
        client.post('http://127.0.0.1:8010/test')

if __name__ == '__main__':
    threading.Timer(1, test_client).start()
    test_server()
```


### Description

A custom middleware sets ContextVar before requests and resets it afterward.
This works as expected for regular HTTP endpoints.
However, when uploading large files (tested >1.5MB on my PC), subsequent requests within 1-2 seconds still access the unreleased ContextVar.

uvicorn==0.35.0

0.116.1

### Description

accepted_answer:
When you run app as `fastapi run test.py --root-path /api/v1`, it's supposed that you run it behind the proxy that strips prefix.
If not, Uvicorn adds the prefix second time and your app gets `http://127.0.0.1:8000/api/v1/api/v1/docs`.

So, you should configure proxy as shown in docs: https://fastapi.tiangolo.com/advanced/behind-a-proxy/#testing-locally-with-traefik

```python
import os

       return # do nothing

    should register a startup event if APP_REGISTER_SOME_STARTUP_EVENT is true or 1.
    """

    app = FastAPI()

```


### Description

Hi there!

I'm trying to test conditional registering of a startup event (conditional because once it is registered this event requires some CPU resources throughout the process lifespan, and I want to be able to control that).

I'm unable to find how to check what startup events have been registered.
I tried the above (`app.router.on_startup`), and I thoroughly searched the internet, FastAPI's codebase, and Starlette's codebase (for the Lifespan context manager), and I wasn't able to find an accessor that allows to get which events have been registered.
I most likely missed something somewhere, but after searching for an hour, I figured it would be better to ask here.

Anyone knows how to/if it is possible to check startup events that have been subscribed on the app?

Thanks!

### Operating System

macOS

### Operating System Details

MacOS Sequioa 15.3.1

### FastAPI Version

0.115.8

### Pydantic Version

2.10.6

### Python Version

3.12

accepted_answer:
Found the source of the issue! It was simply a typo in the env var in the tests 🤦‍♂️ 
This being said, I followed your advice and migrated to the lifespan approach:

`app/main.py`
```python
# app/main.py

from contextlib import asynccontextmanager
from fastapi import FastAPI
from app.lifespan import some_lifespan_ctx

@asynccontextmanager
async def lifespan(app: FastAPI):
    async with some_lifespan_ctx():
        yield

app = FastAPI(lifespan=lifespan)
```

`app/lifespan.py`
```python
import asyncio
import os
from contextlib import asynccontextmanager

counter = [0]  # use list because int is immutable and imported by value, not ref

@asynccontextmanager
async def some_lifespan_ctx():
    task = None
    if os.getenv("ACTIVATE_SOME_LIFESPAN_CTX") in ("true", "1"):
        async def poll():
            while True:
                global counter
                counter[0] += 1
                await asyncio.sleep(60)
        task = asyncio.create_task(poll())

    try:
        yield
    finally:
        if task is not None:
            task.cancel()
            try:
                await task
            except asyncio.CancelledError:
                pass
```

`tests/test_lifespan.py`
```python
import asyncio
import pytest
from app.lifespan import counter, some_lifespan_ctx

# Use pytest-asyncio for async tests.

@pytest.mark.asyncio
async def test_lifespan_ctx_no_poll(monkeypatch):
    """
    should not start a polling task when ACTIVATE_SOME_LIFESPAN_CTX is not set to true or 1.
    """
    # arrange: set polling env var to "0" so no polling task is started.
    monkeypatch.setenv("ACTIVATE_SOME_LIFESPAN_CTX", "0")

    async def fake_sleep(duration):
        raise asyncio.CancelledError()  # kill the loop after one iteration

    monkeypatch.setattr(asyncio, "sleep", fake_sleep)

    # act: run the context manager.
    async with some_lifespan_ctx():
        pass

    # assert: since env var is not in (true, 1), the poll loop shouldn't have run.
    assert counter[0] == 0


@pytest.mark.asyncio
async def test_jwks_poller_ctx_with_poll(monkeypatch):
    """
    should start a polling task when ACTIVATE_SOME_LIFESPAN_CTX is set to true or 1.
    """
    # arrange: set polling env var to "1" so polling task is started.
    monkeypatch.setenv("ACTIVATE_SOME_LIFESPAN_CTX", "1")

    async def fake_sleep(duration):
        raise asyncio.CancelledError()  # kill the loop after one iteration

    monkeypatch.setattr(asyncio, "sleep", fake_sleep)

    # act: run the context manager.
    async with some_lifespan_ctx():
        pass

    # assert: since we raise in sleep, counter should be 1
    assert counter[0] == 1
```

and the tests pass! I haven't tested this simplified version per say, but the real use case has been tested and works :))

Thanks a lot for your help! I'll mark my answer as the resolution, but your help was instrumental! :)

```python
@router.get(
    "/sensor/{sensor_id}"
)  # , response_model=List[MeasurementTimeBucketResponse]
async def get_sensor_measurements(
    sensor_id: int,

            aggregation_interval=interval,
        )
        print(f"DB fetch time: {time.time() - ts}")

        ts = time.time()
        response = [
            MeasurementTimeBucketResponse(**measurement) for measurement in measurements
        ]
        print(f"Pydantic time: {time.time() - ts}")

        ts = time.time()
        json_response = orjson.dumps(
            jsonable_encoder(response), option=orjson.OPT_APPEND_NEWLINE
        )
        print(f"Response time: {time.time() - ts}")

        return Response(content=json_response, media_type="application/json")
    except Exception as e:
        raise HTTPException(
            status_code=status.HTTP_500_INTERNAL_SERVER_ERROR, detail=str(e)
        )


# in my app I use
app.add_middleware(GZipMiddleware)

# and in my front
const response = await api.get(
  "/measurements/sensor/" + route.params.sensorId,
  {
    params: {
      start_time: "2024-01-01T00:00:00",
      end_time: "2025-01-01T00:10:00",
      aggregation_function: "avg",
      interval: "15 minutes",
    },
  }
);
```


### Description

When I query this endpoint I get these timings:

DB fetch time: 0.15195035934448242
Pydantic time: 0.17268824577331543
Response time: 0.5988411903381348

When I try the endpoint in the `/docs`, it simply is too much for the browser to render and get "Maximum call stack size exceeded".

However, in my frontend I see that the whole request takes 2 seconds and 1.8 of it is "waiting for server response".
It is actually faster if I just pass the pydantic objects and let fastapi do the serialization, then the whole request takes 1.6 seconds.

How can I speed this up?




### Operating System

Windows

### Operating System Details

_No response_

### FastAPI Version

0.115.8

### Pydantic Version

2.8.1

### Python Version

3.12

### Additional Context

I'm running the app like this: `uv run uvicorn app.main:app`
accepted_answer:
Hi, I'm not sure if you're still facing this issue or not but just wanted to follow up on this. Sorry for the long delay. From this [blog](https://blog.cloudflare.com/a-question-of-timing/):
> time_starttransfer is just before cURL reads the first byte from the network (it hasn't actually read it yet). This includes the round trip over the network, .....

So your backend server is taking close to 0.47s to calculate the response **before** sending it back completely over the network. I'm not sure how much further you can speed this up without vertically scaling your compute but that's all I can help you with for now without taking a good look at the code. Perhaps there are other ways you can speed up your response calculation time but that's beyond the scope of FastAPI's support. 

To conclude, from the POV of FastApi, I think the only step you can take to speed things up is to dump the JSON yourself instead of relying on FastAPI to do it. Good luck with your project!

title: jsonable_encoder drops exclude_defaults for dict values (propagated for list items)
question_body:
### Summary

`jsonable_encoder` propagates `exclude_defaults` when recursing into **list/tuple/set items**, but silently drops it when recursing into **dict values** (and keys). The two sibling flags `exclude_unset` and `exclude_none` *are* forwarded in that same dict branch, so `exclude_defaults` is the lone omission. As a result the same Pydantic model, with the same flag, encodes differently depending on whether it sits inside a list or a dict.

### Where

`fastapi/encoders.py`, dict branch value recursion:

```python
encoded_value = jsonable_encoder(
    value,
    by_alias=by_alias,
    exclude_unset=exclude_unset,
    exclude_none=exclude_none,          # exclude_defaults is missing here
    custom_encoder=custom_encoder,
    sqlalchemy_safe=sqlalchemy_safe,
)
```

The list branch a few lines below passes `exclude_defaults=exclude_defaults`.

### Reproduction (real `fastapi.encoders.jsonable_encoder`, pydantic 2.x)

```python
from pydantic import BaseModel
from fastapi.encoders import jsonable_encoder

class M(BaseModel):
    a: int = 5
    b: int = 10

jsonable_encoder([M()], exclude_defaults=True)        # [{}]                     -> defaults stripped
jsonable_encoder({"k": M()}, exclude_defaults=True)   # {"k": {"a": 5, "b": 10}} -> NOT stripped
```

Same model, same flag, different result purely by container type.

### Proposed fix

Add `exclude_defaults=exclude_defaults` to the dict-branch recursion (value, and for parity the key), matching the list branch and the two sibling flags already forwarded there:

```python
encoded_value = jsonable_encoder(
    value,
    by_alias=by_alias,
    exclude_unset=exclude_unset,
    exclude_defaults=exclude_defaults,
    exclude_none=exclude_none,
    custom_encoder=custom_encoder,
    sqlalchemy_safe=sqlalchemy_safe,
)
```

### Notes

`exclude_defaults` is a documented public parameter of `jsonable_encoder`. The default FastAPI response path calls it with `exclude_defaults=False`, so this doesn't affect default responses — it surfaces for direct `jsonable_encoder(..., exclude_defaults=True)` use (and internal callers passing the flag). Filing as a Discussion per the contributing guidelines — happy to open a PR with the one-line fix (and a test) if a maintainer would like.
accepted_answer:
Thanks for your intrest!

Let's track it in more general existing discussion: https://github.com/fastapi/fastapi/discussions/15961

### Commit to Help

- [X] I commit to help with one of those options 👆

### Example Code

```python
from typing import Annotated, Any

import pydantic_settings
from fastapi import Depends, FastAPI

app = FastAPI()


class EnvSettings(pydantic_settings.BaseSettings):
    env: str = "LOCAL"


async def get_env_settings() -> EnvSettings:
    return EnvSettings()


async def common_parameters(
    env: Annotated[EnvSettings, Depends(get_env_settings)],
    q: str | None = None,
    skip: int = 0,
    limit: int = 100,
):
    return {"q": q, "skip": skip, "limit": limit, "env": env.env}


@app.get("/users-with-nested-dependency/")
async def read_users_with_nested_dependency(
    commons: Annotated[dict[str, Any], Depends(common_parameters)],
):
    return {"message": f"Hello Users"}


@app.get("/users-with-dependency/")
async def read_users_with_dependency(env: Annotated[EnvSettings, Depends(get_env_settings)]):
    return {"message": f"Hello Users"}


@app.get("/users-without-dependency/")
async def read_users_without_dependency():
    return {"message": "Hello Users"}


if __name__ == "__main__":
    import uvicorn

    uvicorn.run(app, host="0.0.0.0", port=8000)
```


### Description

I have an application which make heavy use of dependencies. I have deeply nested dependencies, since the application has grown. It keeps the code super clean and modular, which is a plus. 

I noticed recently that I wasn't able to hit the load performance I needed. I was tinkering with the code trying to figurate out where the bottleneck could be. To my surprise I noticed that the dependencies was the root cause of it. If I completely removed them from my router definition, I'd achieve very high RPS. As soon as I add one, my RPS would drop. With all of them added, I'd get back to where I started. In essence, I go from 1800 -> 200 RPS. These tests where done in my machine, locally, running the the app with `fastapi run dev`. 

I created an MVP to observe this decay. I added a simple `main.py` with three routes. One without any dependency, a single dependency and a nested dependency. I run the load test on each one of these endpoints individually. I observed very similar behavior. 

![image](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/2fcd7c63-a47e-40c0-b4d1-31868b91619b)

From left to right, without dependency, single dependency and nested dependency run, respectively. We can clearly see the drop in RPS we can produce. I've tried to keep the tests as objective as possible, by running them back to back in the exact same conditions, but feel free to suggested a better testing method. 

I guess my question here is if this is completely expected, since in essence we are calling functions to resolve values at runtime during the request flow? I would expect some degradation of performance, but 10-20% seems extreme. 

If the goal of dependencies is not to instantiate clients and keep code modular, as I am doing in my actual app, please educate me :)

I just wanted to say that you should compare endpoints that do equal job. It's useless to compare the performance of endpoint that doesn't accept any parameters with the endpoint that accepts and validates several parameters.

The following code compares 3 endpoints with equal functionality. And it shows that the difference (average) is very small:

```python
from functools import lru_cache
from typing import Annotated, Any

import pydantic_settings
from fastapi import Depends, FastAPI, Request 

app = FastAPI()


class EnvSettings(pydantic_settings.BaseSettings):
    env: str = "LOCAL"


@lru_cache
def _get_env_settings() -> EnvSettings:
    return EnvSettings()


async def get_env_settings() -> EnvSettings:
    return _get_env_settings()


async def common_parameters(
    env: Annotated[EnvSettings, Depends(get_env_settings)],
    q: str | None = None,
    skip: int = 0,
    limit: int = 100,
):
    return {"q": q, "skip": skip, "limit": limit, "env": env.env}


@app.get("/users-with-nested-dependency/")
async def read_users_with_nested_dependency(
    commons: Annotated[dict[str, Any], Depends(common_parameters)],
):
    return {
        "env": commons["env"],
        "q": commons["q"],
        "skip": commons["skip"],
        "limit": commons["limit"],
    }


@app.get("/users-with-minimal-dependency/")
async def read_users_with_dependency(
    q: str | None = None, skip: int = 0, limit: int = 100
):
    env = _get_env_settings()
    return {
        "env": env,
        "q": q,
        "skip": skip,
        "limit": limit,
    }


@app.get("/users-without-dependencies/")
```

question_body:

### Test Case 1: generic Exception handler + middleware

```python
from typing import Awaitable, Callable
from contextvars import ContextVar

from fastapi import FastAPI, Request
from fastapi.responses import JSONResponse, Response

var: ContextVar[str] = ContextVar("var", default="default")

app = FastAPI()

@app.exception_handler(Exception)
async def handle_exception(request: Request, exc: Exception) -> JSONResponse:
    # Expect: "Bob"
    return JSONResponse({"error": str(exc), "var": var.get()})

@app.get("/error")
async def error() -> dict:
    var.set("Bob")
    raise Exception("Something went wrong!")

@app.middleware("http")
async def set_default_user(
    request: Request, call_next: Callable[[Request], Awaitable[Response]]
) -> Response:
    var.set("Alice")
    response = await call_next(request)
    return response
```


### Description

I’m seeing **two** related problems when using `ContextVar` + FastAPI exception handlers:

1. When I register a generic exception handler (`@app.exception_handler(Exception)`), FastAPI sometimes appears to bypass it and I get the default 500 handler/logs instead.
2. In cases where the generic handler does run, the `ContextVar` value seen in the handler is the one set by middleware (e.g. `"Alice"`) rather than the value set in the endpoint right before the exception (e.g. `"Bob"`). Using a specific handler like `@app.exception_handler(ValueError)` preserves the `ContextVar` value as expected.

This looks like a mismatch in how context is propagated to the generic exception handler and/or the wrong handler layer is catching the exception first.

### Operating System

macOS

### Operating System Details

_No response_

### FastAPI Version

0.118.0

### Pydantic Version

2.11.7

Python 3.12.9

### Additional Context

**Expected response (200):**
`{"error":"Something went wrong!","var":"Bob"}
`

**Actual response (observed):**
`{"error":"Something went wrong!","var":"Alice"}
`
**Server log ([full log](#full-log)):**
```
INFO:     127.0.0.1:60375 - "GET /error HTTP/1.1" 500 Internal Server Error
ERROR:    Exception in ASGI application
Traceback (most recent call last):
  ...
  File ".../test_context_vars.py", line XX, in error
    raise Exception("Something went wrong!")
Exception: Something went wrong!
```

So the response body suggests the handler ran but with lost context, and the logs suggest the default 500 handler got involved.

### Test Case 2 : specific ValueError handler + middleware

```python
from typing import Awaitable, Callable
from contextvars import ContextVar

from fastapi import FastAPI, Request
from fastapi.responses import JSONResponse, Response

var: ContextVar[str] = ContextVar("var", default="default")

app = FastAPI()

@app.exception_handler(ValueError)
async def handle_value_error(request: Request, exc: ValueError) -> JSONResponse:
    # Gets "Bob" as expected
    return JSONResponse({"error": str(exc), "var": var.get()})

@app.get("/error")
async def error() -> dict:
    var.set("Bob")
    raise ValueError("Something went wrong!")

@app.middleware("http")
async def set_default_user(
    request: Request, call_next: Callable[[Request], Awaitable[Response]]
) -> Response:
    var.set("Alice")
    response = await call_next(request)
    return response

```

**Response :**
`{"error":"Something went wrong!","var":"Bob"}`

**log:**
`INFO:     127.0.0.1:61424 - "GET /error HTTP/1.1" 200 OK`

### Test Case 3: catching the exception inside middleware
```python
from typing import Callable, Awaitable
from contextvars import ContextVar
from fastapi import FastAPI, Request
from fastapi.responses import JSONResponse
from starlette.responses import Response

var: ContextVar[str] = ContextVar("var", default="default")
app = FastAPI()

@app.middleware("http")
async def all_exceptions_mw(
    request: Request,
    call_next: Callable[[Request], Awaitable[Response]],
) -> Response:
    token = var.set("Alice")
    try:
        return await call_next(request)
    except Exception as exc:
        # Expected: "Bob" (set in the route before raising)
        # Actual: "Alice"
        return JSONResponse({"error": str(exc), "var": var.get()}, status_code=200)
    finally:
        var.reset(token)

@app.get("/error")
async def error() -> JSONResponse:
    var.set("Bob")
    raise Exception("Something went wrong!")
```

**Response :**
`{"error": "Something went wrong!", "var": "Alice"}  #Excpected Bob`

**log:**
`INFO:     127.0.0.1:61424 - "GET /error HTTP/1.1" 200 OK`

So even though the exception never leaves the middleware (FastAPI’s handler isn’t involved), the context at the point of raising is already lost.

### Test Case 4: Exception handler without middleware
```python
from fastapi import FastAPI, Request
from fastapi.responses import JSONResponse
from contextvars import ContextVar


var: ContextVar[str] = ContextVar("var", default="default")

app = FastAPI()

@app.exception_handler(Exception)
async def handle_exception(request: Request, exc: Exception):
    return JSONResponse({"error": str(exc), "var": var.get()})


@app.get("/error")
async def error():
    var.set("Bob")
    raise Exception("Something went wrong!")
```
**Response :**
`{"error": "Something went wrong!", "var": "Bob"}`

**Server log ([full log](#full-log)):**
```
INFO:     127.0.0.1:60375 - "GET /error HTTP/1.1" 500 Internal Server Error
ERROR:    Exception in ASGI application
Traceback (most recent call last):
  ...
  File ".../test_context_vars.py", line XX, in error
    raise Exception("Something went wrong!")
Exception: Something went wrong!
```

The custom handler does execute and the context (`"Bob"`) is preserved. But the ServerErrorMiddleware still logs the exception, even though the handler handled it — suggesting that the generic Exception handler registration isn’t preventing Starlette’s default error handling from running.

### Temporary Patch

After further debugging, I found that patching `FastAPI.build_middleware_stack()` seems to fix the **part** of the issue.

```python
def build_middleware_stack(self) -> ASGIApp:
    # Duplicate/override from Starlette to add AsyncExitStackMiddleware
    # inside of ExceptionMiddleware, inside of custom user middlewares
    debug = self.debug
    error_handler = None
    exception_handlers: dict[Any, ExceptionHandler] = {}

   for key, value in self.exception_handlers.items():
-      if key in (500, Exception):
+      if key in (500):
           error_handler = value
       else:
           exception_handlers[key] = value

   middleware = (
       [Middleware(ServerErrorMiddleware, handler=error_handler, debug=debug)]
       + self.user_middleware
       + [
           Middleware(ExceptionMiddleware, handlers=exception_handlers, debug=debug),
    # Add FastAPI-specific AsyncExitStackMiddleware for closing files.
    # Before this was also used for closing dependencies with yield but
    # those now have their own AsyncExitStack, to properly support ...

```
> This patch comments out the extraction of the generic Exception / 500 handlers
and avoids wrapping the user middlewares with ServerErrorMiddleware.

| Test case | Fixed by patch | 
|:-----------|:--------------:|
|Case 1|✅|
|Case 2 |✅|
|Case 3 |❌|
|Case 4 |✅|

the [middleware-level `try/except` case](#additional-test-catching-the-exception-inside-middleware-still-loses-context) (catch in middleware) still reads `"Alice"` (❌), meaning the exception is still being raised/executed in a different async context than the one in `call_next()`.

I hope that with this last explanation I’m able to clear up all your doubts.
What you wrote about what you understood is all correct; I’d only add, for completeness, that the `BaseHTTPMiddleware` (the one you use via a decorator) was designed and implemented to provide a simple, ready-to-use tool, but over time it has led to a number of problems or limitations. Personally, I almost never use it and I always prefer a pure ASGI middleware.

As for the additional questions you asked, I’ll share a comment on each of the scenarios you used as examples.
Before starting with the examples, let me share a bit more information.

In **FastAPI** (and partly in **Starlette**), a middleware stack is built in the following order:
`ServerErrorMiddleware`, `UserMiddleware1`, `UserMiddleware2`, `…`, `UserMiddlewareN`, `ExceptionMiddleware`.

The execution flow of a request is **LIFO**.
The **ServerErrorMiddleware** is generally the first to receive the request but also the last to emit the response.
The **ExceptionMiddleware**, instead, is the last one (right before the endpoint) to receive the request and the first to emit the response.
All user-defined middleware are inserted between **ServerErrorMiddleware** and **ExceptionMiddleware**.

### Purpose of the **ServerErrorMiddleware** and the **ExceptionMiddleware**:

The **ServerErrorMiddleware** is generally responsible for always emitting a response from the application, even in the case of an exception. This middleware, whose code you can see [here](https://github.com/Kludex/starlette/blob/main/starlette/middleware/errors.py), includes an exception handler that generates a `500 Internal Server Error` response when an unhandled exception occurs.

It allows you to define your own exception handler for this middleware by referring to the base exception, e.g."
```python
@app.exception_handler(Exception)
```

The **ExceptionMiddleware**, on the other hand, is the middleware that lets you handle possible exceptions raised in the endpoints through dedicated handlers. Examples include `HTTPException` or `RequestValidationError`, as well as custom exceptions that are then handled by a dedicated handler. At the moment, it isn’t possible to add a generic exception handler here, because that would “disable” all the other handlers.

### Test case explanations

#### Test Case 1: generic Exception handler + middleware

```python
from typing import Awaitable, Callable
from contextvars import ContextVar

from fastapi import FastAPI, Request
from fastapi.responses import JSONResponse, Response

var: ContextVar[str] = ContextVar("var", default="default")

app = FastAPI()

@app.exception_handler(Exception)
async def handle_exception(request: Request, exc: Exception) -> JSONResponse:
    # Expect: "Bob" --> You should expect Alice not bob here. This is executed from ServerErrorMiddleware
    return JSONResponse({"error": str(exc), "var": var.get()})

@app.get("/error")
async def error() -> dict:
    var.set("Bob")
    raise Exception("Something went wrong!")

@app.middleware("http")
async def set_default_user(
    request: Request, call_next: Callable[[Request], Awaitable[Response]]
) -> Response:
    var.set("Alice")
    response = await call_next(request)  # this will run in a child level
    return response
```

The generic exception handler is added to the **ServerErrorMiddleware**, Alice is set before `await call_next(request)` [ref](https://github.com/Kludex/starlette/blob/main/starlette/middleware/base.py#L112-L189) so Alice is at the same level of **ServerErrorMiddleware**.
Bob is set in the endpoint that is a child level of Alice and will be lost back on the middleware.
You will see a stacktrace mentioning even collapse_excgroups. Output and log is expected and correct.


#### Test Case 3: catching the exception inside middleware

``` python
from typing import Callable, Awaitable
from contextvars import ContextVar
from fastapi import FastAPI, Request
from fastapi.responses import JSONResponse
from starlette.responses import Response

var: ContextVar[str] = ContextVar("var", default="default")
app = FastAPI()

@app.middleware("http")
async def all_exceptions_mw(
    request: Request,
    call_next: Callable[[Request], Awaitable[Response]],
) -> Response:
    token = var.set("Alice")
    try:
        return await call_next(request)
    except Exception as exc:
        # Expected: "Bob" (set in the route before raising)
        # Actual: "Alice" --> this is correct
        return JSONResponse({"error": str(exc), "var": var.get()}, status_code=200)
    finally:
        var.reset(token)

@app.get("/error")
async def error() -> JSONResponse:
    var.set("Bob")
    raise Exception("Something went wrong!")

```
The exception will never reach the **ServerErrorMiddleware** so you will not see the exception logged, same logic about context log.
The response  is expected.


#### Test Case 4: Exception handler without middleware

```python
from fastapi import FastAPI, Request
from fastapi.responses import JSONResponse
from contextvars import ContextVar


var: ContextVar[str] = ContextVar("var", default="default")

app = FastAPI()

@app.exception_handler(Exception)
async def handle_exception(request: Request, exc: Exception):
    return JSONResponse({"error": str(exc), "var": var.get()})


@app.get("/error")
async def error():
    var.set("Bob")
    raise Exception("Something went wrong!")

```
No **HTTPMiddlewareBase** here, so this time the flow is all on one level, the exception handler is run from **ServerErrorMiddleware**, this exception will be logged but the stack is much shorter.
Bob is in the response.

### Conclusion
I don’t see any inconsistency, neither in the logging nor in the loss of context. There are clear rules that provide predictability and reproducibility of results. I understand it can feel a bit tricky at first, but I don’t see anything unexpected or that would require further investigation.
I hope this has been useful and addressed your concerns.

```python
from fastapi import FastAPI

class HttpExpectedError(BaseModel):

  message: str = Field(..., description="Error message for human")

    return self.model_dump()
```

### Example Code

```python
async def my_middleware(request: Request, call_next):
    ...
    response = await call_next(request)
    print(type(response))
    ...
    return response
```


### Description

Why does the above _always_ print `starlette.middleware.base._StreamingResponse`? It prints that even for non-streaming requests. And I cannot access the original type, why?? :cry: :disappointed: 

### Operating System

Linux

_No response_

0.115.12

2.8.2

### Python Version

3.11.8

_No response_
accepted_answer:
I'll try to give a more detailed answer.

Once FastAPI creates the response: JSONResponse, Response, a custom subclass, etc. , it still has to encode and transmit it according to the ASGI spec. At that point FastAPI calls the response as an ASGI app: await response(scope, receive, send).

Middlewares that implement the pure ASGI interface (`__call__(self, scope, receive, send)`) only see ASGI messages (http.response.start, http.response.body, …): status code, headers, body chunks. The original Python object and its concrete class are not included in those messages. So when you say the "type is lost," is because the middleware no longer has a reference to the original subclass unless you explicitly keep it somewhere.

BaseHTTPMiddleware wraps things for you, but it buffers and rebuilds a generic Response. If you need to know the specific response class in middleware, you have to persist it yourself. Note: using BaseHTTPMiddleware is discouraged (https://github.com/encode/starlette/discussions/2160)

So: the server doesn’t "forget/lost" the type; it’s just not part of the ASGI event stream that middlewares see by default.

Said that,

> Why does the above always print starlette.middleware.base._StreamingResponse?

Because you’re using BaseHTTPMiddleware. It wraps the original response in its own internal _StreamingResponse to make streaming/body buffering simpler. So when you print(type(response)) inside that middleware, you see the wrapper, not your original JSONResponse, HTMLResponse, etc.

The same happens on the request side: the incoming request is exposed as _CachedRequest.

This is not an issue in Fast API.
2. There are millions of people who are using OpenAPI for their production loads and I'm fairly certain that a lot of them are using the upsert operation without any issue. So this problem looks very specific to your code otherwise there would have been at least 10s of thousands of issues related to this on the repo.

If you want to generate the `user_id` on behalf of the client, then that's a `POST` operation altogether as it represents the creation of a new resource rather than an update or insertion of an existing one identified by a path parameter.

title: 0.137.0: `APIRoute.tags` invisible to type checkers in generate_unique_id_function (regression from #15745)
question_body:
### First check

- I searched existing discussions and issues — no existing report for this.
- This is about a **type-checker regression in 0.137.0**, not a runtime bug (runtime is unaffected).

### Summary

In **0.137.0**, the documented `generate_unique_id_function` pattern from [Advanced → Generate Clients](https://fastapi.tiangolo.com/advanced/generate-clients/) — which reads `route.tags` — now fails static type checking. Type checkers report that `APIRoute` has no attribute `tags`, even though the docs still show exactly this code and it works fine at runtime.

This appears to be an unintended side-effect of #15745 ("Refactor internals to preserve APIRouter and APIRoute instances"): `APIRoute.__init__` was changed to delegate state-setting to a helper that receives `self` cast to the `_APIRouteLike` Protocol, and `APIRoute` itself no longer carries a class-level `tags` annotation. So the attribute is still assigned at runtime, but it's invisible to type checkers looking at the `APIRoute` type.

### Reproducible example

This is the docs' own example (`docs_src/generate_clients/tutorial003_py310.py`):

```python
from fastapi import FastAPI
from fastapi.routing import APIRoute


def custom_generate_unique_id(route: APIRoute) -> str:
    return f"{route.tags[0]}-{route.name}"


app = FastAPI(generate_unique_id_function=custom_generate_unique_id)
```

Running a type checker (`ty`) over it on 0.137.0:

```
error[unresolved-attribute]: Object of type `APIRoute` has no attribute `tags`
 --> repro.py:6:15
  |
6 |     return f"{route.tags[0]}-{route.name}"
  |               ^^^^^^^^^^
```

At runtime the same code builds the app and generates operation IDs correctly — only the static type surface is affected. `route.name` resolves fine; only `route.tags` is missing.

### Expected behavior

`route.tags` should remain visible to type checkers as a public attribute of `APIRoute` (it's part of the documented public callback contract), as it was in 0.136.x where `APIRoute.__init__` assigned `self.tags = tags or []` directly.

### Environment

- FastAPI: **0.137.0**
- Python: 3.14
- Type checker: `ty` 0.0.49 (also reproduces with strict Pyright per the same root cause); mypy may differ
- OS: macOS

### Possible fix

Add the lost class-level annotation back to `APIRoute` (e.g. `tags: list[str | Enum]`) so it matches what the `_APIRouteLike` Protocol already declares. Happy to open a PR if that direction is welcome.

Thanks for FastAPI! 🙏
accepted_answer: This should be fixed in https://github.com/fastapi/fastapi/pull/15765 , available in FastAPI 0.137.1, just released :rocket:

title: Pydantic's UUID generate wrong JSON schema
accepted_answer:
It comes from Pydantic.

```py
class MyModel(BaseModel):
    id: UUID4
    name: str

print(MyModel.model_json_schema())
```
Results in:
```json
{
    "properties": {
        "id": {"format": "uuid4", "title": "Id", "type": "string"},
        "name": {"title": "Name", "type": "string"}
    },
    "required": ["id", "name"],
    "title": "MyModel",
    "type": "object"
}
```

Not sure why it's this way. `uuid4` is not a valid value for `fromat` field according to Json Schema spec.

> we can see that independently on the UUIDn used, it will always generate {'title': 'A', 'type': 'string', 'format': 'uuid'} for the json schema.

The above statement is wrong.
Look at the `base_schema['properties']['a']['format'] = expected_schema` line. It overrides the `format` field in expected `base_schema` with values like `uuid`, `uuid1`, `uuid2`, etc..

Anyway, if this is an issue, then it's an issue on Pydantic's side

title: Dependency keeps going after response returns when there exists any backgroud tasks.
question_body:
### Issue Content

```python
import asyncio

from fastapi import Depends, BackgroundTasks, FastAPI
from fastapi.responses import PlainTextResponse


app = FastAPI()

async def dep():
    yield
    print("dep done")

async def task():
    await asyncio.sleep(5)
    print("task done")

@app.get("/test", response_class=PlainTextResponse, tags=["test"], dependencies=[Depends(dep)])
async def test(bk: BackgroundTasks):
    bk.add_task(task)
    return "OK"
```

When access test endpoint, Both fastapi 0.128.0 and 0.133.0 have this behavior:

1. Response returns
2. print "dep done"
3. print "task done".

But in fastapi 0.115.12:

1. print "dep done"
2. Response returns
3. print "task done".

When the dependency is a database transaction, transaction is not committed after response returns, data changes are not accessable before backgroud tasks completion.
accepted_answer:
Please, follow the template and don't open issues.

---
The behavior of dependencies with yield was changed in FastAPI [0.121.0](https://fastapi.tiangolo.com/release-notes/#01210).
See: https://fastapi.tiangolo.com/tutorial/dependencies/dependencies-with-yield/#early-exit-and-scope

In short - you can configure it to work as it used to work using `scope="function"`:
```py
Depends(dep, scope="function")
```

title: Return type vs ORJSONResponse: does generic return type as dict[str, Any] use the Pydantic serializer efficently?
question_body:
### First Check

- [X] I already checked if it is not related to FastAPI but to [Swagger UI](https://github.com/swagger-api/swagger-ui).
- [X] I already checked if it is not related to FastAPI but to [ReDoc](https://github.com/Redocly/redoc).

### Commit to Help

- [X] I commit to help with one of those options 👆

### Example Code

```python
from fastapi import FastAPI

app = FastAPI()

@app.get("/example")
def example() -> dict[str, Any]:
return {"hello": "world"}
```


### Description

Hi FastAPI team,
 
I have a question regarding the current response serialization behavior, especially after the recent ORJSONResponse deprecation guidance.
 
While investigating the warning:
 
> FastAPI now serializes data directly to JSON bytes via Pydantic when a return type or response model is set
 
I inspected the implementation of `fastapi.routing.serialize_response()` in the version currently installed in my environment and found the following logic:
 
```python
async def serialize_response(...):
if field:
...
serializer = field.serialize_json if dump_json else field.serialize
return serializer(...)
else:
return jsonable_encoder(response_content)
```
 
To better understand when the Pydantic serialization path is selected, I temporarily patched `serialize_response()` and logged the value of `field` during request execution.
 
For an endpoint defined only with a generic return type:
 
```python
@app.get("/example")
def example() -> dict[str, Any]:
return {"hello": "world"}
```
 
the runtime output was:
 
```text
ModelField(
field_info=FieldInfo(annotation=dict[str, Any], required=True),
name='Response_example',
mode='serialization',
config=None
)
```
 
This seems to indicate that FastAPI creates a response `ModelField` even for generic return types such as `dict[str, Any]`, and therefore enters the `field.serialize()` path instead of the `jsonable_encoder()` path.
 
Based on this, I would like to confirm a few points:
 
1. Is this behavior intentional and considered part of the public/expected behavior of FastAPI?
 
2. Can users rely on a generic return type like:
 
```python
-> dict[str, Any]
-> list[dict[str, Any]]
-> list[Any]
```
 
to activate the Pydantic response serialization path, even when no explicit `response_model` is provided?
 
3. From a performance perspective, should users generally prefer:
 
```python
@app.get("/")
def endpoint() -> dict[str, Any]:
...
```
 
over:
 
```python
@app.get("/", response_class=ORJSONResponse)
def endpoint():
...
```
 
given the current deprecation warning around `ORJSONResponse`?
 
4. Are there any meaningful performance differences between:
```python
-> dict[str, Any]
```
 
and
 
```python
-> MyPydanticModel
```
 
with regard to the generated serializer and serialization speed?
 
5. Would it be worth clarifying this point in the documentation?
 
The current wording mentions "return type or response model", which many readers (including me initially) could interpret as primarily referring to Pydantic models. However, from the implementation and runtime behavior it appears that even generic typed returns such as `dict[str, Any]` participate in the Pydantic serialization path.
 
Thanks for the clarification, and for all the work on FastAPI.

### Operating System

Linux

### Operating System Details

_No response_

### FastAPI Version

0.140.7

### Pydantic Version

2.13.4

### Python Version

Python 3.13.0

### Additional Context

_No response_
accepted_answer:
Your reading of the code is right. Numbers below are from your exact versions — FastAPI 0.140.7, Pydantic 2.13.4, Python 3.13.

**1 and 2 — intentional, and yes you can rely on generics**

Any return annotation FastAPI can build a `TypeAdapter` for produces a response field, generics included:

```
route annotation                  response_field  response_class  fast path
-> (none)                         none            default         False
-> dict[str, Any]                 yes             default         True
-> list[dict[str, Any]]           yes             default         True
-> list[Any]                      yes             default         True
-> Any                            yes             default         True
-> MyModel                        yes             default         True
-> dict[str, Any] + ORJSONResponse yes            ORJSON          False
-> (none) + ORJSONResponse        none            ORJSON          False
```

Even bare `-> Any` gets one. The only ways to end up on the `jsonable_encoder` branch are to omit the annotation or to return a `Response` object yourself.

**3 — prefer the return type, and don't set both**

This is the part worth knowing. From `fastapi/routing.py` in 0.140.7:

```python
# Use the fast path (dump_json) when no custom response
# class was set and a response field with a TypeAdapter
# exists. Serializes directly to JSON bytes via Pydantic's
# Rust core, skipping the intermediate Python dict +
# json.dumps() step.
use_dump_json = response_field is not None and isinstance(
    response_class, DefaultPlaceholder
)
```

Passing `response_class=ORJSONResponse` means `response_class` is no longer a `DefaultPlaceholder`, so `use_dump_json` is `False` — you keep the response field but drop to `field.serialize` → Python objects → `ORJSONResponse.render()`. Setting both is the *slowest* of the three arrangements, not the fastest. (Both `ORJSONResponse` and `UJSONResponse` carry `@deprecated` in `fastapi/responses.py`, so the warning you hit is real, not advisory folklore.)

**4 — a model is faster than `dict[str, Any]`, and both beat the encoder path badly**

Serialization only, 20,000 iterations, best of 3, 20-key flat dict with one nested value:

```
 4.9 us   -> MyModel                        serialize_json  (fast path)
 6.1 us   -> dict[str, Any]                 serialize_json  (fast path)
13.3 us   -> dict[str, Any]                 serialize + json.dumps
48.4 us   no annotation + ORJSONResponse    jsonable_encoder + orjson.dumps
53.8 us   no annotation                     jsonable_encoder + json.dumps
 0.8 us   orjson.dumps(payload)             raw, for reference
```

The model wins by roughly 25% because `Any` has no static schema — pydantic-core has to infer each value's type at runtime, while a declared model compiles a specialized serializer.

The bigger point is the ~8x gap to the encoder rows, and it explains the deprecation: the expensive part was never `json.dumps` vs `orjson.dumps`, it was `jsonable_encoder` walking the object graph in Python. That's also why `ORJSONResponse` only ever bought ~10% here — it optimized the cheap half of the work. Absolute numbers scale with payload size and shape; the ratios held across runs.

**5 — agreed, worth documenting**

"return type or response model" is accurate but reads as if it means Pydantic models specifically. Two additions would have saved you the source dive: that *any* return annotation qualifies, `dict[str, Any]` included, and that setting a custom `response_class` silently opts you out of the fast path. The second one is the surprising half — it's easy to assume the two optimizations stack. Happy to open a docs PR if a maintainer wants it.
</content>

```python
import uvicorn
from fastapi import Depends, FastAPI
from pydantic import BaseModel, ConfigDict

app = FastAPI()

class TestParams(BaseModel):

if __name__ == "__main__":

# Then run curl localhost:8000/
```

### Description

We're attempting to use Pydantic's defer_build functionality to improve developer env boot times by delaying pydantic model building to when we actually need to use it. It appears that fastapi gets confused by the defer_build param (see repro). The error returned is:
`{"detail":[{"type":"missing","loc":["query","data"],"msg":"Field required","input":null}]}`

This does not reproduce when the model_config is commented out. I'm surprised no one else has reported this so far based on searching, so filing a bug here. Not super clear if it's a pydantic or fastapi issue here - it feels like given what pydantic claims to happen with defer_build=True, fastapi should make sure to call model_build() on any pydantic model classes being used in route construction calls?

Python 3.11.7

accepted_answer:
Hello @davidhao3300,
the official supported way to use Model in query is the following, and actually support even your use-case.

``` python
import uvicorn
from typing import Annotated
from fastapi import FastAPI, Query
from pydantic import BaseModel, ConfigDict

app = FastAPI()

class TestParams(BaseModel):
    model_config = ConfigDict(defer_build=True)
    x: int = 1

@app.get("/")
async def index_route(
    params: Annotated[TestParams, Query()]
) -> None:
    return

if __name__ == "__main__":
    uvicorn.run(app, host="0.0.0.0", port=8000)
```

If you use `Depends` like you did, FastApi will try to inspect the signature of a model that has not been created yet.

title: Regression in 0.118.2: BeforeValidator not called for query parameters with Annotated types
question_body:
### First Check

- [X] I added a very descriptive title here.
- [X] I used the GitHub search to find a similar question and didn't find it.
- [X] I searched the FastAPI documentation, with the integrated search.
- [X] I already searched in Google "How to X in FastAPI" and didn't find any information.
- [X] I already read and followed all the tutorial in the docs and didn't find an answer.
- [X] I already checked if it is not related to FastAPI but to [Pydantic](https://github.com/pydantic/pydantic).
- [X] I already checked if it is not related to FastAPI but to [Swagger UI](https://github.com/swagger-api/swagger-ui).
- [X] I already checked if it is not related to FastAPI but to [ReDoc](https://github.com/Redocly/redoc).

### Commit to Help

- [X] I commit to help with one of those options 👆

### Example Code

```python
"""Demonstrates BeforeValidator regression in FastAPI 0.118.2"""
import dataclasses
from typing import Annotated, Optional
from fastapi import FastAPI
from pydantic import BeforeValidator, PlainSerializer
from starlette.testclient import TestClient


# Custom class (similar to MongoDB ObjectId, Version objects, etc.)
@dataclasses.dataclass(frozen=True)
class StudyVersion:
    """Represents a study version like '8.8' or '880'"""
    major: int
    minor: int
    patch: int = 0

    @classmethod
    def parse(cls, value):
        if value is None:
            return None
        if isinstance(value, StudyVersion):
            return value
        # Parse "8.8" format
        if isinstance(value, str) and "." in value:
            parts = value.split(".")
            return cls(int(parts[0]), int(parts[1]) if len(parts) > 1 else 0)
        # Parse 880 -> (8, 8, 0)
        value_int = int(value)
        return cls(value_int // 100, (value_int % 100) // 10, value_int % 10)

    def __str__(self):
        return f"{self.major}.{self.minor}" if self.minor else f"{self.major}"


# Type definition (common pattern in production code)
StudyVersionStr = Annotated[
    StudyVersion,
    BeforeValidator(StudyVersion.parse),
    PlainSerializer(str)
]

app = FastAPI()


@app.post("/studies", response_model=None)
def create_study(name: str, version: Optional[StudyVersionStr] = None):
    """
    In 0.118.1: version is correctly parsed to StudyVersion instance
    In 0.118.2: version stays None, BeforeValidator is not called
    """
    print(f"version parameter: {version!r}")
    return {
        "name": name,
        "version": str(version) if version else None,
    }


if __name__ == "__main__":
    import fastapi
    print(f"Testing with FastAPI {fastapi.__version__}")

    client = TestClient(app)
    response = client.post("/studies?name=test&version=8.8")
    print(f"Response: {response.json()}")

    # Expected in 0.118.1:
    #   version parameter: StudyVersion(major=8, minor=8, patch=0)
    #   Response: {'name': 'test', 'version': '8.8'}  ✅

    # Actual in 0.118.2:
    #   version parameter: None
    #   Response: {'name': 'test', 'version': None}  ❌
```


### Description

## Description

  In FastAPI **0.118.1**, `BeforeValidator` works correctly with `Optional[Annotated[T, BeforeValidator(...)]]` query parameters:
  - Query parameter `?version=8.8` is parsed to `StudyVersion(major=8, minor=8, patch=0)` ✅
  - The validator function is called as expected

  In FastAPI **0.118.2**, the same code **silently breaks**:
  - Query parameter `?version=8.8` is ignored, endpoint receives `version=None` ❌
  - `BeforeValidator` is **not called at all**
  - No error raised at startup, validation is completely bypassed

  ### Root cause

  This regression appears to be introduced by **PR #12942** ("Fix tagged discriminated union not recognized as body field").

  While the PR correctly fixes discriminated unions, it inadvertently breaks `BeforeValidator` execution for query parameters with `Annotated` types.

  ### Impact

  This is a **silent regression** affecting production code:
  - Custom version objects (e.g., StudyVersion)
  - Custom ID types with parsing logic
  - Any domain-specific value objects using `BeforeValidator`

  The application starts without errors, but validation logic is completely bypassed and endpoints receive `None` instead of validated objects.


### Operating System

Linux

### Operating System Details

_No response_

### FastAPI Version

0.118.2

### Pydantic Version

2.12.0

### Python Version

3.11.13

### Additional Context

_No response_
accepted_answer:
Since your actual type (`StudyVersion`) is complex, FastAPI treats it as `Body` parameter, but you send it as `Query`, that's why it's `None`.
For me it's more strange that it worked before 0.118.2. 

So, it looks like it worked because of the bug, and that bug was fixed by https://github.com/fastapi/fastapi/pull/12942.

For simple types it works as expected:
```py
from typing import Annotated, Optional
from fastapi import FastAPI
from pydantic import BeforeValidator
from starlette.testclient import TestClient

MyAnnotatedType = Annotated[str, BeforeValidator(lambda x: f"p_{x}")]

app = FastAPI()

@app.post("/")
def post_(param: Optional[MyAnnotatedType] = None):
    return {"param": param}

def test_():
    client = TestClient(app)
    response = client.post("/", params={"param": "value"})
    assert response.status_code == 200, response.text
    assert response.json() == {"param": "p_value"}
```

question_body:

### Commit to Help

- [X] I commit to help with one of those options 👆

### Example Code

```python
from enum import StrEnum

from fastapi import FastAPI
from pydantic import BaseModel, Field


class MessageEventType(StrEnum):
    alpha = "alpha"
    beta = "beta"


class MessageEvent(BaseModel):
    event_type: MessageEventType = Field(default=MessageEventType.alpha)
    output: str


class MessageOutput(BaseModel):
    body: str = ""
    events: list[MessageEvent]


class Message(BaseModel):
    id: str
    input: str
    output: MessageOutput


app = FastAPI(title="Minimal FastAPI App", version="1.0.0")


@app.post("/messages", response_model=Message)
async def create_message(input_message: str) -> Message:
    return Message(
        input=input_message,
        output=MessageOutput(body=f"Processed: {input_message}"),
    )


if __name__ == "__main__":
    openapi_spec = app.openapi()
    for c in list(openapi_spec.get("components", {}).get("schemas", {}).keys()):
        print(c)
```


### Description

## Issue Summary

Take the minimal example provided above, run with `fastapi==0.118.3` and it will produce:

```
HTTPValidationError
Message
MessageEvent
MessageEventType
MessageOutput
ValidationError
```

Now run the same code with `fastapi==0.119.0` and it will produce:

```
HTTPValidationError
Message
MessageEvent
MessageEventType
MessageOutput-Input
MessageOutput-Output
ValidationError
```

Note how `MessageOutput` is now suffixed unnecessarily as: `MessageOutput-Input` and `MessageOutput-Output`. This seems unexpected considering the changes made between   `v0.118.3` and `v0.119.0`

## Minor Tweak

One minor tweak to the example and this issue goes away. Remove the enum from `MessageEvent`: 

```python
class MessageEvent(BaseModel):
    output: str
```

Run again and the issue is no longer there.

```
HTTPValidationError
Message
MessageEvent
MessageOutput
ValidationError
```

## TLDR

Why does the presence of an enum value on `MessageEvent` create a bifurcated OpenAPI schema definition for `MessageOutput` and why does this issue only start happening in `fastapi==0.119.0`?

macOS

15.6.1 (24G90)

### FastAPI Version

0.119.0

### Pydantic Version

2.12.0

### Python Version

Python 3.13.1

_No response_

Thank you all for the discussion! :raised_hands: :coffee: 

I added an issue here: https://github.com/fastapi/fastapi/issues/14247 just for completeness.

It should be fixed in https://github.com/fastapi/fastapi/pull/14246, just relased in FastAPI 0.120.2. :tada: 

Thanks for the great report @walsha2, I used it with some minor tweaks as the test for the fix PR. :sunglasses:

title: Consider Pydantic serialization for exception handlers before deprecating ORJSONResponse
question_body:
Following the discussion in #14964, deprecating `ORJSONResponse` and `UJSONResponse` might be premature since exception handlers can't benefit from the new Pydantic serialization introduced in #14962.

Currently, exception handlers must return a `Response` object, which means they fall back to stdlib `json.dumps` via `JSONResponse`, the exact use case where `ORJSONResponse` was providing free performance gains.

Two possible paths forward:

1. Use Pydantic serialization in `JSONResponse`

`JSONResponse` could use `TypeAdapter.dump_json` internally instead of `json.dumps`. Though this might impose constraints on the accepted content types.

2. Support typed returns in exception handlers

Allow exception handlers to return dicts or Pydantic models directly, similar to regular route handlers:

```python
class MyErrorBody(BaseModel):
    message: str

@app.exception_handler(MyError, status_code=status.HTTP_422_UNPROCESSABLE_ENTITY)
async def _(request: Request, exception: MyError) -> MyErrorBody:
    return MyErrorBody(message=str(exception))
```

This would enable Pydantic serialization for exception responses and feed the OpenAPI schema generation with error response types, which is currently not possible.
accepted_answer:
For now, if you worry about the performance for errors / exception handlers, you could create a custom response with your serialization, it's 4 lines of code: https://fastapi.tiangolo.com/advanced/custom-response/#custom-response-class

And you could also use something other than orjson, or a different format, etc.

title: Problem with multiple Query in view of an endpoint
question_body: ### First Check - [X] I added a very descriptive title here. - [X] I used the GitHub search to find a similar question and didn't find it. - [X] I searched the FastAPI documentation, with the integrated search. - [X] I already searched in Google "How to X in FastAPI" and didn't find any information. - [X] I already read and followed all the tutorial in the docs and didn't find an answer. - [X] I already checked if it is not related to FastAPI but to [Pydantic](https://github.com/pydantic/pydantic). - [X] I already checked if it is not related to FastAPI but to [Swagger UI](https://github.com/swagger-api/swagger-ui). - [X] I already checked if it is not related to FastAPI but to [ReDoc](https://github.com/Redocly/redoc). ### Commit to Help - [X] I commit to help with one of those options 👆 ### Example Code ```python see below ``` ### Description Hi all! p.s. If you have some filtering/sorting/pagination approach please share) I'm trying to develop `filtering/ordering/pagination` functionality for FastAPI applications. For now I'm facing difficulty with separating filtering and sorting. The code below generates undesirable swagger: ```python from fastapi import FastAPI, Query from pydantic import BaseModel from sqlalchemy import Select, create_engine, MetaData, select from sqlalchemy.orm import DeclarativeBase, Mapped, mapped_column app = FastAPI() url = "postgresql+psycopg2://postgres:postgres@localhost:5432/database" engine = create_engine(url, echo=True) class Base(DeclarativeBase): metadata = MetaData() class User(Base): __tablename__ = "users" id: Mapped[int] = mapped_column(primary_key=True) first_name: Mapped[str] last_name: Mapped[str] class FilterSet(BaseModel): first_name: str | None def filter_queryset(self, query: Select) -> Select: conditions = self.model_dump(exclude_unset=True) # apply ordering return query class Ordering(BaseModel): ordering: list[str] | None = None def order_queryset(self, query: Select) -> Select: self.ordering # apply ordering return query @app.get("/") async def index(filterset: FilterSet = Query(), ordering: Ordering = Query()): query = select(User) query = filterset.filter_queryset(query) query = ordering.order_queryset(query) # request database ``` The bad swagger: Is it possible to fix it without combining FilterSet and Ordering classes into a single class? ### Operating System macOS ### Operating System Details _No response_ ### FastAPI Version 0.116.1 ### Pydantic Version 2.10.6 ### Python Version 3.11 ### Additional Context _No response_
accepted_answer:
FastAPI doesn't support multiple query models. You need to combine them into one model.
One approach is using multiple inheritance:
```python
class QueryParameters(FilterSet, Ordering):
    pass

@app.get("/")
async def index(params: QueryParameters = Query()):
    query = select(User)
    query = params.filter_queryset(query)
    query = params.order_queryset(query)
```

Could you explain the purpose of using context manager in your use case? I mean, why do you need to decorate `get_hi` with `@asynccontextmanager`?

You can fix your code by just removing `@asynccontextmanager` decorator. FastAPI will recognize the generator and create the context manager out of it.

Regarding #11143: as I see it, that issue is not about passing context managers to `Depends`, but about using context managers inside dependencies with `yield` (the behavior of such dependencies was changed in v0.106.0).
