title: Different sub-application behaviour when using FastAPI(root_path=...) vs --root-path CLI option
question_body:
### First Check - [X] I added a very descriptive title here. - [X] I used the GitHub search to find a similar question and didn't find it. - [X] I searched the FastAPI documentation, with the integrated search. - [X] I already searched in Google "How to X in FastAPI" and didn't find any information. - [X] I already read and followed all the tutorial in the docs and didn't find an answer. - [X] I already checked if it is not related to FastAPI but to [Pydantic](https://github.com/pydantic/pydantic). - [X] I already checked if it is not related to FastAPI but to [Swagger UI](https://github.com/swagger-api/swagger-ui). - [X] I already checked if it is not related to FastAPI but to [ReDoc](https://github.com/Redocly/redoc). ### Commit to Help - [X] I commit to help with one of those options 👆 ### Example Code ```python from fastapi import FastAPI, Request from starlette.routing import get_route_path root_app = FastAPI() sub_app = FastAPI() root_app.mount("/subapp", sub_app) @root_app.get("/test") async def root_test(path: str, request: Request): return { "app": "root", "root_path": request.scope.get("root_path", ""), "path": request.scope.get("path", ""), "route_path": get_route_path(request.scope), } @sub_app.get("/test") async def sub_test(path: str, request: Request): return { "app": "sub", "root_path": request.scope.get("root_path", ""), "path": request.scope.get("path", ""), "route_path": get_route_path(request.scope), } ``` ### Description I am creating a FastAPI application that is served behind a proxy which strips part of the path, so I've been following the [Proxy with a stripped path prefix](https://fastapi.tiangolo.com/advanced/behind-a-proxy/#proxy-with-a-stripped-path-prefix) docs. I am also using mounted sub-applications to handle API versioning (e.g. mounted at `/v1` and `/v2` for separate docs). Initially, I was using the `root_path` parameter in the FastAPI constructor to configure the stripped-path prefix, which works as expected for the root application, but I experienced unexpected behaviour adding the sub-applications. --- `tl;dr` According to the [FastAPI docs](https://fastapi.tiangolo.com/advanced/behind-a-proxy/#setting-the-root-path-in-the-fastapi-app): > Passing the `root_path` to `FastAPI` would be the equivalent of passing the `--root-path` command line option to Uvicorn or Hypercorn. However, my experience has shown that these configuration methods result in different behaviour for the request scope `path` which seems to break route matching in mounted sub-applications when using the `root_path` parameter. --- **With no root path configuration:**
```GET /test - 200 OK ✅``` ```GET /subapp/test - 200 OK ✅```
```json json { "app": "root", "root_path": "", "path": "/test", "route_path": "/test", } ``` ```json json { "app": "sub", "root_path": "/subapp", "path": "/subapp/test", "route_path": "/test", } ```
**OpenAPI schema:** `/openapi.json` and `/subapp/openapi.json` With no root path configuration, the behaviour is as expected. --- **Root path configured via FastAPI CLI with `--root-path="/api"`:**
```GET /test - 200 OK ✅``` ```GET /subapp/test - 200 OK ✅```
```json json { "app": "root", "root_path": "/api", "path": "/api/test", "route_path": "/test", } ``` ```json json { "app": "sub", "root_path": "/api/subapp", "path": "/api/subapp/test", "route_path": "/test", } ```
```GET /api/test - 404 Not Found ❌``` ```GET /api/subapp/test - 404 Not Found ❌```
```json json { "detail": "Not Found" } ``` ```json json { "detail": "Not Found" } ```
**OpenAPI schema:** `/api/openapi.json` and `/api/subapp/openapi.json` When configuring the root path via the FastAPI CLI option, the routes can be accessed at `localhost:8000/test` and `localhost:8000/subapp/test` as expected, since the `/api` root path would be stripped by the proxy. It is not possible to access the routes by including the root path in the requests when using the CLI option (as shown by the 404s). The OpenAPI schema is served with the root path prefixed so the Swagger UI can access it from outside the proxy (as described in the [FastAPI docs](https://fastapi.tiangolo.com/advanced/behind-a-proxy/#check-the-docs-ui)) --- **Root path configured via FastAPI constructor with `root_path="/api"`:**
```GET /test - 200 OK ✅``` ```GET /subapp/test - 404 Not Found ❌```
```json json { "app": "root", "root_path": "/api", "path": "/test", "route_path": "/test", } ``` ```json json { "detail": "Not Found" } ```
```GET /api/test - 200 OK ✅``` ```GET /api/subapp/test - 200 OK ✅```
```json json { "app": "root", "root_path": "/api", "path": "/api/test", "route_path": "/test", } ``` ```json json { "app": "root", "root_path": "/api/subapp", "path": "/api/subapp/test", "route_path": "/test", } ```
**OpenAPI schema:** `/api/openapi.json` and `/api/subapp/openapi.json` Note that `/docs` and `/api/docs` work (and both fetch the OpenAPI JSON schema correctly), but `/subapp/docs` doesn't work – only `/api/subapp/docs` works. When configuring the root path via the FastAPI `root_path` constructor parameter, the root FastAPI app route can be accessed at `localhost:8000/test` as expected, **BUT** the sub-application route can no longer be accessed without the root path in the URL. Additionally, the behaviour continues to deviate since now it is possible to access the root app route by including the root path in the request which was not possible with the CLI option. The OpenAPI schema is served with the root path prefixed so the Swagger UI can access it from outside the proxy, but now the UI does not show a "Failed to load API definition" Fetch error. ### Operating System macOS ### Operating System Details macOS Sequoia 15.1.1 (24B91) ### FastAPI Version 0.135.1 ### Pydantic Version 2.11.4 ### Python Version 3.12.9 ### Additional Context This behaviour is described in another [discussion post](https://github.com/fastapi/fastapi/discussions/11959) from 2024, but I wasn't sure if necroposting in the comments was appropriate. I thought I would make a new discussion and hopefully be able to resolve the old discussion along with this one.
accepted_answer:
> Passing the `root_path` to FastAPI would be the equivalent of passing the `--root-path` command line option to Uvicorn or Hypercorn.

This statement in docs is not correct.
In fact, you should:
* use `--root-path` when you run app behind a proxy which **strips** part of the path
* use `root_path` parameter in the `FastAPI` constructor when you run app behind a proxy that **doesn't strip** part of the path

I opened PR to fix docs: https://github.com/fastapi/fastapi/pull/14238

### Example Code

```python
def set_log_attributes(
    request: Request | WebSocket, attrs: dict[str, Any]
) -> dict[str, Any]:
    if not isinstance(request, Request):
        return attrs
    ...
    credentials = http_bearer(request)
    auth_session = authenticator(credentials=credentials)
    if auth_session.user_id:
        attrs["user_id"] = auth_session.user_id
    return attrs

logfire.instrument_fastapi(
    app, capture_headers=False, request_attributes_mapper=set_log_attributes
)
```


### Description

What is the reason to have HTTPBase and derived classes __call__ method async?

https://github.com/fastapi/fastapi/blob/master/fastapi/security/http.py

My motivation is that I'm using logfire with fastapi integration that has custom function as `request_attributes_mapper`
https://github.com/pydantic/logfire/blob/d3682562f08344537ec9114f47f52631c2b6b364/logfire/_internal/main.py#L1012

Inside this function, I'd like to use my security_scheme as 
```
bearer_security = HTTPBearer(auto_error=False)
```
to retrieve credentials and after - the user_id
but because of async nature I need to make async function synchronous 

### Operating System

macOS

### Operating System Details

_No response_

### FastAPI Version

0.115.8

### Pydantic Version

2.10.6

### Python Version

Python 3.12.1

### Additional Context

_No response_
accepted_answer:
Hello @gurobokum,

> What is the reason to have HTTPBase and derived classes call method async?

Fastapi is an asynchronous framework, all subclasses of `HTTPBase ` can be used as dependency and for this reason they are async. Each not async dependency is executed in a separated thread to avoid blocking the main loop, so make it sync, would be only inefficient.

About your case: since logfire for fastapi is based on [OpenTelemetry FastAPI Instrumentation](https://opentelemetry-python-contrib.readthedocs.io/en/latest/instrumentation/fastapi/fastapi.html) would be better to attach the user info to the request or a span and read them from there instead of reprocessing the header twice.

title: Admin Panel for FastAPI (Similar to Django Admin)
question_body:
Hello everyone,

I’m looking for a robust and stable admin panel solution for FastAPI, similar to Django Admin for Django. Ideally, it should be well-maintained, production-ready, and capable of handling complex applications.

I'm open to both free and paid options, as long as they are reliable. If you have experience with any such tools, I’d really appreciate your insights and recommendations.

Thanks in advance!
accepted_answer:
@apiguy123 You have several options based on the ORM you are using. If you use SqlAlchemy, SQLModel, Tortoise ORM, etc. you can try 
[Fastadmin](https://github.com/vsdudakov/fastadmin), [Starlette-admin](https://github.com/jowilf/starlette-admin) or [SQLAdmin](https://github.com/aminalaee/sqladmin). If you are using Piccolo ORM you can try [Piccolo Admin](https://github.com/piccolo-orm/piccolo_admin). Hope that helps.

### Example Code



### Description

It would be great to auto-document [marimo apps](https://docs.marimo.io/guides/deploying/programmatically/) that take query parameters the way that FastAPI does that, using [pydantic query models](https://fastapi.tiangolo.com/tutorial/query-param-models/) and [OpenAPI](https://fastapi.tiangolo.com/tutorial/metadata).

Your Suggestion for Changes
As marimo are Starlette, not FastAPI apps, they don't take the docs_url parameters to `App()` that build the OpenAPI schemas and the /docs endpoints. [This ](https://fastapi.tiangolo.com/how-to/extending-openapi/#modify-the-openapi-schema)also doesn't work:

```
from fastapi.openapi.utils import get_openapi

openapi_schema = get_openapi(
    title="Custom title",
    version="2.5.0",
    summary="This is a very custom OpenAPI schema",
    description="Here's a longer description of the custom **OpenAPI** schema",
    routes=app.routes,  # mounted Marimo routes do not show up here
)
```

If it is possible to build OpenAPI docs, would you please suggest how?

https://github.com/marimo-team/marimo/issues/4878

### Operating System

Linux, Other

### Operating System Details

any

### FastAPI Version

0.115.11

### Pydantic Version

2.33.2

### Python Version

3.12

### Additional Context

_No response_
accepted_answer:
I can explain.

The solution you are talking about is:
```
from fastapi import FastAPI, Request, Query
from fastapi.responses import RedirectResponse
from marimo import create_asgi_app
from pathlib import Path
from pydantic import BaseModel, Field
from typing import Annotated, Literal
from urllib.parse import urlencode


app = FastAPI()


class FilterParams(BaseModel):
    limit: int = Field(100, gt=0, le=100)
    offset: int = Field(0, ge=0)
    order_by: Literal["created_at", "updated_at"] = "created_at"
    tags: list[str] = []


@app.get("/items")
async def marimo_items(
    request: Request, filter_query: Annotated[FilterParams, Query()]
):
    query_params = urlencode(filter_query.model_dump(), doseq=True)
    return RedirectResponse(url=f"/items/?{query_params}")


server = create_asgi_app(include_code=True, quiet=False)
notebooks_dir = Path(__file__).parent.parent / "notebooks"

for filename in notebooks_dir.iterdir():
    if filename.suffix == ".py":
        app_name = filename.stem
        server = server.with_app(path=f"/{app_name}", root=filename)


app.mount("/", server.build())
```

So, here we have FastApi app with `GET` endpoint with path `/items` and marimo app, that has endpoint with another path (`/items/`).

For FastAPI `/items` and `/items/` are different paths. FastAPI shows nicely-looking docs for `/items` because that endpoint function was annotated properly.
But this `/items` endpoint just redirects all requests to `/items/` (endpoint of marimo app).

title: `bytes` field inside Pydantic model with `Form()` fails — UploadFile not read
question_body:
### First Check

- [X] I added a very descriptive title here.
- [X] I used the GitHub search to find a similar question and didn't find it.
- [X] I searched the FastAPI documentation, with the integrated search.
- [X] I already searched in Google "How to X in FastAPI" and didn't find any information.
- [X] I already read and followed all the tutorial in the docs and didn't find an answer.
- [X] I already checked if it is not related to FastAPI but to [Pydantic](https://github.com/pydantic/pydantic).
- [X] I already checked if it is not related to FastAPI but to [Swagger UI](https://github.com/swagger-api/swagger-ui).
- [X] I already checked if it is not related to FastAPI but to [ReDoc](https://github.com/Redocly/redoc).

### Commit to Help

- [X] I commit to help with one of those options 👆

### Example Code

```python
from typing import Annotated
from fastapi import FastAPI, Form
from fastapi.testclient import TestClient
from pydantic import BaseModel

app = FastAPI()

class UploadForm(BaseModel):
    name: str
    file: bytes

@app.post("/upload/")
async def upload(data: Annotated[UploadForm, Form()]):
    return {"name": data.name, "size": len(data.file)}

client = TestClient(app)
response = client.post(
    "/upload/",
    files={"file": ("test.txt", b"hello world", "text/plain")},
    data={"name": "test"},
)
print(response.status_code)
print(response.json())


---
```


### Description

```
I am using a Pydantic BaseModel with Form() to group form fields together. 
When one of the fields is annotated as `bytes`, FastAPI does not call 
`read()` on the uploaded file and returns a 422 error instead.

What I expect:
- Status 200, FastAPI automatically reads the UploadFile into bytes,
  exactly as it does when `bytes` is a standalone File() parameter.

What actually happens:
- Status 422, `bytes_type` validation error. The raw UploadFile object 
  is passed directly to Pydantic without being read first.

This works fine (standalone):

    @app.post("/works/")
    async def works(file: bytes = File()):
        return {"size": len(file)}  # ✅ 200

This breaks (inside a Pydantic model):

    class UploadForm(BaseModel):
        file: bytes

    @app.post("/breaks/")
    async def breaks(data: Annotated[UploadForm, Form()]):
        return {"size": len(data.file)}  # ❌ 422

Affected annotations inside a Pydantic Form model:

| Annotation          | Works? |
|---------------------|--------|
| file: UploadFile    |  Yes |
| file: UploadFile|None | Yes |
| file: list[UploadFile] |  Yes |
| file: bytes         |  No  |
| file: bytes | None  |  No  |
| file: list[bytes]   |  No  |

I looked into the source code. The issue is in `_extract_form_body()` 
in `fastapi/dependencies/utils.py`. The guard:

    isinstance(field_info, params.File)

is always False for fields extracted from a Pydantic model because 
those fields have plain Pydantic FieldInfo, not params.File.
So `read()` is never called on the UploadFile.

I would be happy to work on a fix if this is confirmed.
```

---

## Operating System:
```
Windows
```

## FastAPI Version:
```
0.135.1

### Operating System

Windows

### Operating System Details

Windows 11

### FastAPI Version

0.135.1

### Pydantic Version

2.12.5

### Python Version

Python 3.11.9

### Additional Context

```
The standalone `bytes = File()` parameter works correctly.
The bug only occurs when `bytes` is declared inside a Pydantic 
BaseModel used with Form().

I also checked that `UploadFile`, `Optional[UploadFile]`, and 
`list[UploadFile]` inside a Pydantic Form model all work fine — 
only the `bytes` annotation is affected.

I have looked at the source code and I believe I can fix this.
I would be happy to submit a PR if this is confirmed.
accepted_answer:
Declaring file upload fields using Pydantic model is not officially supported ([see comment to closed PR](https://github.com/fastapi/fastapi/pull/14343#issuecomment-3600534954)).

To make your example work, you need to add `File()` annotation to `file` field:

```py
class UploadForm(BaseModel):
    name: str
    file: Annotated[bytes, File()]
```

And specify `media_type="application/x-www-form-urlencoded"` as follows to make schema correct:

```py
@app.post("/upload/")
async def upload(data: Annotated[UploadForm, Form(media_type="application/x-www-form-urlencoded")]):
    return {"name": data.name, "size": len(data.file)}
```

One more time: this is not officially supported. You can use it on your own risk)

title: Regeneration OpenAPI schema without restarting FastAPI
question_body:
### First Check

- [X] I added a very descriptive title here.

- [X] I searched the FastAPI documentation, with the integrated search.

- [X] I already checked if it is not related to FastAPI but to [Swagger UI](https://github.com/swagger-api/swagger-ui).
- [X] I already checked if it is not related to FastAPI but to [ReDoc](https://github.com/Redocly/redoc).

### Commit to Help

- [X] I commit to help with one of those options 👆

### Example Code

```python
def regenerate_openapi_schema():
    """Customize and regenerate the OpenAPI schema."""
    def custom_openapi():
        if not app.openapi_schema:
            # Regenerate the OpenAPI schema
            app.openapi_schema = app.openapi()
        return app.openapi_schema

    # Overwrite the original openapi method
    app.openapi = custom_openapi
```


### Description

I'm trying to find a way to force FastAPI (for example when SQLAlchemy ORM detects change) to regenerate the OpenAPI schema and update `openapi.json` along with Swagger UI when something is changed in the routes. Like dynamic ENUM's or whatever.

The new schema (`app.openapi_schema`) is generated perfectly with the changes present, compared to the schema after app start. But it wont appear as a new one in the `/docs` endpoint, no matter I do. I know that the schema is cached.

I know this is asked before, but without clear resolution. I am aware that the schema generation at the app startup is the expected and normal behavior and regeneration of schema without restarting the app is quite an edge case. But I find it a necessary one.

Thank you!

### Operating System

Windows, macOS

### Operating System Details

_No response_

### FastAPI Version

0.115.12

### Pydantic Version

2.10.6

### Python Version

3.12

### Additional Context

_No response_
accepted_answer:
Hello @TanelS,
there is not an official and supported way to do it.
Keeping that in mind, consider the following as a "workaround".

**General considerations:**

Far small changes that do not impact on route definition, validation. etc. you can modify directly the `app.openapi_schema` definition. For example if your want to change the title, version, some decription and so on. This operation will not require any reload.

Changes to route definitions, validation, etc., are more complex to handle because modifying the OpenAPI specs alone is not enough to affect FastAPI's request handling flow — unless you have a truly dynamic validation process in place.

**Workaround**
The app.openapi_schema is not the only thing FastAPI caches — it also caches the routes along with their dependencies. So even if you update your route information and regenerate the API schema, it will still use the 'cached' version of your routes to generate the schema.

What can you do?

    - Add the same endpoint again with its updated definition.
    - Invalidate the OpenAPI schema by setting app.openapi_schema = None.
    - Regenerate the OpenAPI schema (it will now reflect the latest routes).
    - Remove the old version of the endpoint.

Why does this work?

    - Each route is appended to the router’s internal route list.
    - For every incoming request, FastAPI iterates through this list from top to bottom and executes the first matching route.
    - OpenAPI schema generation follows the same order — but when duplicate paths exist, the last one overrides the previous definition in the schema.
    - Therefore, to fully replace a route, you must remove the earlier version (i.e. the first occurrence of that path/method combo).
      At that point, your newly added endpoint becomes both the active one for requests and the one reflected in the docs.

**Note**:

All of these changes must be made on the main FastAPI app. Any modifications applied directly to an APIRouter after it has been included in the app will have no effect.
This is an unofficial workaround, so it may break or behave differently in future FastAPI versions — don’t rely on it being officially supported.
Whenever possible, prefer using real dynamic types and properly updating the OpenAPI specs through officially supported means. Only consider hot-reloading or runtime patching when restarting the app is truly not an option.

Hope this helps.

### Example Code

```python
import typing as t

import fastapi
import fastapi.testclient
from pydantic import AliasChoices, BaseModel, Field


class Model(BaseModel):
    items: t.Annotated[list[str], Field(validation_alias=AliasChoices("items_alias", "items"))]


app = fastapi.FastAPI()


@app.get("/")
def root(
    model: t.Annotated[Model, fastapi.Query()],
) -> Model:
    return model


client = fastapi.testclient.TestClient(app)


def request_with_params(params: dict):
    result = client.get("/", params=params)
    assert result.status_code == 200, (result.status_code, result.json())


request_with_params({"items": "asdf"})
request_with_params({"items_alias": ["asdf", "asd2"]})
request_with_params({"items_alias": "asdf"})  # <-- this one fails
```


### Description

I've created a Query-Model that contains a list field, so that the field may be provided in multiple times. I want to provide multiple aliases for this field. When I provide the field under the default name, all is well. When I provide multiple values under the alias, all is well. However, when I provide a single value under the alias, I get a validation error.

I would expect the validation to succeed with a single value under the alias name

### Example Code

```python
from typing import Annotated, Literal

from fastapi import FastAPI, Query
from pydantic import BaseModel, Field

app = FastAPI()


class FilterParams(BaseModel):
    limit: int = Field(100, gt=0, le=100)
    offset: int = Field(0, ge=0)
    order_by: Literal["created_at", "updated_at"] = "created_at"
    tags: list[str] = []


class MoreParams(BaseModel):
    extra_param: str = Field(
        ...,
        description="An extra parameter",
    )

        None,
        alias="identifier",
        description="Another Parameter",
    )

@app.get("/items/")
async def read_items(
        filter_params: Annotated[FilterParams, Query()],
        more_params: Annotated[MoreParams, Query()]
    ) -> str:
        return "NA"
```


### Description

I'm having trouble getting multiple query parameter objects to work using the method described in the docs. 
When I try the example code included in this post the OpenAPI docs look like this:
![image](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/33eddc47-3a2d-4c8f-95f3-0cdbcd7c9288)


I've had this working in past versions of FastAPI using Depends() like this:

```
from typing import Literal

from fastapi import Depends, FastAPI
from pydantic import BaseModel, Field

app = FastAPI()


class FilterParams(BaseModel):
    limit: int = Field(100, gt=0, le=100)
    offset: int = Field(0, ge=0)
    order_by: Literal["created_at", "updated_at"] = "created_at"
    tags: list[str] = []


class MoreParams(BaseModel):
    extra_param: str = Field(
        ...,
        description="An extra parameter",
    )
    another_param: str = Field(
        None,
        alias="identifier",
        description="Another Parameter",
    )

@app.get("/items/")
async def read_items(
        filter_params: FilterParams = Depends(),
        more_params: MoreParams = Depends()
    ) -> str:
        return "NA"

```
However, this doesn't seem to work correctly. Note that the "tags" parameter is missing from the docs.
![image](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/86e32dae-b1af-4351-841c-a100b27693a9)


I'm not sure what I'm doing wrong here and to be honest I am not understanding the difference in semantics between using Query() and using Depends().

Any help will be much appreciated. Thank you.

### Operating System

Linux

### Operating System Details

_No response_

### FastAPI Version

0.115.7

### Pydantic Version

2.10.6

### Python Version

3.12.6

_No response_
accepted_answer:
Hello @tfrangoullides, for now is not possible to use multiple models for Query params,
this is duplicate of https://github.com/fastapi/fastapi/discussions/13448.

About the difference between Depends and Query (Oversimplify).
The first one is used to declare a dependency, is not directly related to query but is used sometimes for query params based on how Fastapi construct the dependency chain.
Query before v115 were used to identify 1 to 1 a single query params. From 115 you can use it to identify all fields of a Pydantic Models as query params.

### Example Code

```python
from fastapi import FastAPI
from pydantic import BaseModel
from fastapi import HTTPException, Depends


router = FastAPI()


class UpdateUser(BaseModel):
    rank: int


def validate_body(args: UpdateUser):
    if args.rank > 100:
        raise HTTPException(status_code=400, detail="Invalid rank")

    return args


@router.patch("/user/{user_id}", operation="user.update_user")
def update_user(args: UpdateUser, args_from_dependency: UpdateUser = Depends(validate_body)):
    assert args is args_from_dependency
```


### Description

When endpoint `PATCH` `/user/{user_id}` from example above is requested - FastAPI creates two `UpdateUser` instances(probably, runs validation twice for each parameter).

Expected behavior is that the FastAPI don't revalidates body, if it is already validated

### Operating System

Linux

### Operating System Details

Linux 6.1.0-37-amd64 #1 SMP PREEMPT_DYNAMIC Debian 6.1.140-1 (2025-05-22) x86_64 GNU/Linux

0.110.1

2.7.0

3.11.2

_No response_
accepted_answer:
I agree that we shouldn't validate request parameters twice.

The main reason is that it gives us duplicated error messages in case of validation error.
Several related discussions:
* https://github.com/fastapi/fastapi/discussions/8669
* https://github.com/fastapi/fastapi/discussions/8659
* https://github.com/fastapi/fastapi/discussions/9005

As I see it, we should validate parameters once and then use its deep-copy for each instance.

If it's important in your use-case that only one instance is used, you can use the chain of dependencies (create dependency that returns parameter and use it in other dependencies) to achieve this

title: Annotations with generic type not recognized as Query without explicit Query(...) as default arguement
question_body:
### First Check

- [X] I added a very descriptive title here.
- [X] I used the GitHub search to find a similar question and didn't find it.
- [X] I searched the FastAPI documentation, with the integrated search.

- [X] I already checked if it is not related to FastAPI but to [Pydantic](https://github.com/pydantic/pydantic).
- [X] I already checked if it is not related to FastAPI but to [Swagger UI](https://github.com/swagger-api/swagger-ui).
- [X] I already checked if it is not related to FastAPI but to [ReDoc](https://github.com/Redocly/redoc).

### Commit to Help

- [X] I commit to help with one of those options 👆

### Example Code

```python
from enum import StrEnum
from typing import Annotated, TypeVar

from fastapi import FastAPI, Query
from pydantic import BeforeValidator

T = TypeVar("T")


def map_empty_to_null(val: T) -> T | None:
    if val == "":
        return None
    return val


GenericQuery = Annotated[Annotated[T, BeforeValidator(map_empty_to_null)], Query]


class Foo(StrEnum):
    A = "a"
    B = "b"
    C = "c"


app = FastAPI()


@app.get("/")
async def get_home(
    q: GenericQuery[str | None] = None,
    foo: GenericQuery[list[Foo] | None] = Query(default=None),
    bar: GenericQuery[list[Foo] | None] = None,
):
    return {"q": q, "foo": foo}


if __name__ == "__main__":
    import uvicorn

    uvicorn.run(app, host="0.0.0.0", port=8000)
```


### Description

My Understanding from above code
> In FastAPI, parameters are classified as query, path, or body depending on how they’re declared. Normally, adding Query(...) makes FastAPI treat it as a query param, while plain = None without Query defaults to body (for non-path args). given that, foo and bar should have same side effect.

Here, I wrapped the types in a reusable `GenericQuery` annotation. For `foo`, I still passed `Query(default=None)`, and FastAPI correctly treats it as a query param. For `bar`, I relied on the annotation alone, but FastAPI ignores it and incorrectly places bar in the request body

### Operating System

macOS

### Operating System Details

_No response_

### FastAPI Version

0.116.1

### Pydantic Version

2.8.2

### Python Version

Python 3.12.5

### Additional Context

_No response_
accepted_answer:
Hi @ManiMozaffar 

I suggest changing your `GenericQuery` signature to the following

```python
GenericQuery = Annotated[T, BeforeValidator(map_empty_to_null), Query()]
```

This signature has two improvements
1. You don't need to nest annotations, since the runtime will flatten it anyway, expanding the nested annotation into the outermost one.
2. It fixes your issue

The issue is caused by passing to FastAPI a _function_, while the proposed annotation passes it a Query object.

When initialising the API, FastAPI parses all the parameters of the endpoint functions, casting them as queries, path parameters, etc. When passing a Query object in a query annotation, FastAPI recognises it correctly easily. With your annotation, FastAPI discards the function and makes a best guess of what the parameter could be. As it happens `q` is parsed as a query, but `bar` is recognised as a body parameter because the data type is a list. `foo` on the other hand works as expected because you do pass to the parameter a `Query` object.

I tested the following endpoint with the modified annotation and it works as expected.

```python
@app.get("/")
async def get_home(
    q: GenericQuery[Foo | None] = None,
    foo: GenericQuery[list[Foo] | None] = None,
    bar: GenericQuery[list[Foo] | None] = None,
) -> dict[str, GenericQuery[list[Foo] | None] | GenericQuery[Foo | None]]:
    return {"q": q, "foo": foo, "bar": bar}
```

Hope this helps!

title: Use `return` instead of `continue`  in fastapi/_compat/shared.py at L150-200?
question_body:
### First Check

- [X] I added a very descriptive title here.
- [X] I used the GitHub search to find a similar question and didn't find it.
- [X] I searched the FastAPI documentation, with the integrated search.
- [X] I already searched in Google "How to X in FastAPI" and didn't find any information.

- [X] I already checked if it is not related to FastAPI but to [Pydantic](https://github.com/pydantic/pydantic).
- [X] I already checked if it is not related to FastAPI but to [Swagger UI](https://github.com/swagger-api/swagger-ui).
- [X] I already checked if it is not related to FastAPI but to [ReDoc](https://github.com/Redocly/redoc).

### Commit to Help

- [X] I commit to help with one of those options 👆

### Example Code

```python
"""fastapi\_compat\shared.py, L150"""
...

def is_bytes_sequence_annotation(annotation: Any) -> bool:
    origin = get_origin(annotation)
    if origin is Union or origin is UnionType:
        at_least_one = False
        for arg in get_args(annotation):
            if is_bytes_sequence_annotation(arg):
                at_least_one = True
                continue
        return at_least_one
    return field_annotation_is_sequence(annotation) and all(
        is_bytes_or_nonable_bytes_annotation(sub_annotation)
        for sub_annotation in get_args(annotation)
    )


def is_uploadfile_sequence_annotation(annotation: Any) -> bool:
    origin = get_origin(annotation)
    if origin is Union or origin is UnionType:
        at_least_one = False
        for arg in get_args(annotation):
            if is_uploadfile_sequence_annotation(arg):
                at_least_one = True
                continue
        return at_least_one
    return field_annotation_is_sequence(annotation) and all(
        is_uploadfile_or_nonable_uploadfile_annotation(sub_annotation)
        for sub_annotation in get_args(annotation)
    )
...
```


### Description

While reading fastapi/_compat, I noticed a small detail.

The continue seems unnecessary (no code after it in the loop body). This could be simplified (and short-circuited) without changing behavior, e.g.:
- return any(is_bytes_sequence_annotation(arg) for arg in get_args(annotation))
- or an early-return loop.

Is there any historical or compatibility reason to keep the current pattern?

### Operating System

Windows

### Operating System Details

_No response_

### FastAPI Version

0.118.0

### Pydantic Version

2.11.10

### Python Version

3.12

### Additional Context

_No response_
accepted_answer:
**Short answer:** There is no behavioral difference here. The `continue` is redundant because the loop body does nothing after it. This can be simplified to an early return or to `any(...)`, which also short-circuits.

#### Why it is safe

* The recursive call has no side effects.
* Current code scans all union args and accumulates a boolean. Returning early or using `any(...)` preserves semantics while avoiding extra recursion.
* This pattern matches similar helpers that already use comprehension utilities.

#### Minimal refactor

```diff
diff --git a/fastapi/_compat/shared.py b/fastapi/_compat/shared.py
index abcdef0..1234567 100644
--- a/fastapi/_compat/shared.py
+++ b/fastapi/_compat/shared.py
@@ -150,17 +150,11 @@ def is_bytes_sequence_annotation(annotation: Any) -> bool:
-    origin = get_origin(annotation)
-    if origin is Union or origin is UnionType:
-        at_least_one = False
-        for arg in get_args(annotation):
-            if is_bytes_sequence_annotation(arg):
-                at_least_one = True
-                continue
-        return at_least_one
+    origin = get_origin(annotation)
+    if origin is Union or origin is UnionType:
+        return any(is_bytes_sequence_annotation(arg) for arg in get_args(annotation))
     return field_annotation_is_sequence(annotation) and all(
         is_bytes_or_nonable_bytes_annotation(sub_annotation)
         for sub_annotation in get_args(annotation)
     )
 
@@ -170,17 +164,11 @@ def is_uploadfile_sequence_annotation(annotation: Any) -> bool:
-    origin = get_origin(annotation)
-    if origin is Union or origin is UnionType:
-        at_least_one = False
-        for arg in get_args(annotation):
-            if is_uploadfile_sequence_annotation(arg):
-                at_least_one = True
-                continue
-        return at_least_one
+    origin = get_origin(annotation)
+    if origin is Union or origin is UnionType:
+        return any(is_uploadfile_sequence_annotation(arg) for arg in get_args(annotation))
     return field_annotation_is_sequence(annotation) and all(
         is_uploadfile_or_nonable_uploadfile_annotation(sub_annotation)
         for sub_annotation in get_args(annotation)
     )
```

#### Optional alternative (early return loop)

```python
if origin in (Union, UnionType):
    for arg in get_args(annotation):
        if is_bytes_sequence_annotation(arg):
            return True
    return False
```

#### Compatibility note

`UnionType` handles the `|` syntax on Python 3.10+. The change does not affect that logic. No API changes, only a local readability and micro-perf improvement.

title: ContextVars in sync vs async dependencies
accepted_answer:
> The TL;DR appears to be that FastAPI treats synchronous dependencies in a separate thread to the one handling the request, thereby causing issues with the way ContextVar handles values internally. The same issue is not present with asynchronous dependencies.

This is not a bug, and is expected behaviour. FastAPI makes the assumption that a sync dependency has blocking code in it (otherwise why not use async) since FastAPI is an async first framework it spawns these dependencies onto a thread pool so as not to block the event loop. This will have implications for context vars.

All three solutions are valid and effectively equivalent. accepted_answer:
You've already answered to your own question)

Do you think it will it be clear if we add the following clarification to docs?

## Multiple middleware execution order

When you add multiple middlewares using either `@app.middleware()` decorator or `app.add_middleware()` method, each new middleware wraps the application, forming a stack. The last middleware added is the *outermost*, and the first is the *innermost*.

On the request path, the *outermost* middleware runs first.

On the response path, it runs last.

For example:

```Python
app.add_middleware(MiddlewareA)
app.add_middleware(MiddlewareB)
```

This results in the following execution order:

* **Request**: MiddlewareB → MiddlewareA → route

* **Response**: route → MiddlewareA → MiddlewareB

This stacking behavior ensures that middlewares are executed in a predictable and controllable order.

### Example Code

```python
import logging
from logging.handlers import RotatingFileHandler
from fastapi import FastAPI, Request

logger = logging.getLogger("app")
logger.setLevel(logging.INFO)

handler = RotatingFileHandler(
    "app.log",
    maxBytes=5 * 1024 * 1024,
    backupCount=3,
    encoding="utf-8",
)

formatter = logging.Formatter(
    "%(asctime)s | %(levelname)s | %(name)s | %(message)s"
)
handler.setFormatter(formatter)
logger.addHandler(handler)

app = FastAPI()

@app.middleware("http")
async def log_requests(request: Request, call_next):
    logger.info(f"{request.method} {request.url.path}")
    response = await call_next(request)
    logger.info(f"status={response.status_code}")
    return response

@app.get("/ping")
async def ping():
    logger.info("Ping")
    return {"status": "ok"}
```


### Description

I’m looking for best practices for using a middleware logger together with internal (application-level) loggers in FastAPI, but I can’t find clear information about possible issues when logging to file(s) while running the app **with multiple workers**.

Are there any problems with file logging when using multiple Uvicorn workers?
Should I rely on Uvicorn’s built-in loggers (uvicorn.error, uvicorn.access),
and do they handle file write races automatically, or do I need to take care of this myself?

Do I need to add a unique identifier (PID) to the log file name to avoid race conditions, or should I avoid file logging when using workers?

The same question applies to running multiple Docker containers/instances: should I explicitly add a prefix or identifier to the log file name, or there is any solution to handle it automatically?

### Operating System

Linux

### Operating System Details

Ubuntu

### FastAPI Version

0.128

### Pydantic Version

2.12

### Python Version

3.11

### Additional Context

You can use my example of code, or any other - stand your ground

Many thanks
accepted_answer:
There are real problems with file logging when you run multiple Uvicorn workers (--workers N).

Each worker is a separate OS process. Stdlib handlers like FileHandler / RotatingFileHandler are thread-safe, but not multi-process safe. Multiple processes can interleave lines and break rotation (double-rotate, lost logs, rename clashes).

Uvicorn’s loggers (uvicorn.error, uvicorn.access) don’t fix this automatically. They’re just normal Python loggers configured by Uvicorn; if you point them at a file handler, you still have the same race unless you add a safe mechanism.

Best practice (especially in Docker/K8s): log to stdout/stderr and let the platform collect/rotate (Docker logging driver, journald, Loki/ELK, etc.).

If you must log to files on a single host:
- Use a multi-process-safe handler (file locking), e.g. concurrent-log-handler’s ConcurrentRotatingFileHandler
- Use QueueHandler/QueueListener (one writer process/thread).

As a simpler fallback: write one file per worker (PID in filename), then aggregate later.
Multiple containers/instances: don’t write all of them into the same shared file. Use stdout aggregation, or unique filenames per instance.

```python
def weak_lru_cache(maxsize=1, typed=False, ttl=None):
    """LRU Cache decorator that keeps a weak reference to self

    Warning: When used in a class, the class should implement __eq__(self, other) and __hash__(self) methods

    Source: https://stackoverflow.com/a/55990799"""

    def wrapper(func):
        @functools.lru_cache(maxsize, typed)
        def _func(_self, *args, ttl_hash=None, **kwargs):
            del ttl_hash  # Unused parameter, but kept for compatibility
            return func(_self(), *args, **kwargs)

        @functools.wraps(func)
        def inner(self, *args, **kwargs):
            return _func(weakref.ref(self), *args, ttl_hash=_get_ttl_hash(ttl), **kwargs)

        return inner
```

### Description

In the latest version of Glances (https://github.com/nicolargo/glances/releases/tag/v4.3.2), we add an LRU cache to optimize a route (see code). In most of the case it works as expected (unitary test is ok: https://github.com/nicolargo/glances/blob/v4.3.2/tests/test_restful.py#L70).

Unfortunately, when Glances is integrated in Home Assistant, it crashs with the following error:

    httpx.RemoteProtocolError: peer closed connection without sending complete message body (received 0 bytes, expected 29904)

See detail here: https://github.com/nicolargo/glances/issues/3238

When i comment the LRU cache:

    #@weak_lru_cache(maxsize=1, ttl=1)
    ...

Then everything work fine....

Any idea where the issue came from ?

Linux

accepted_answer:
Hello @nicolargo,

I cloned your project and debugged the issue so I could give you a more detailed answer.

I suspected from the start that the problem was not caching the computed value, but rather caching the entire response instance.
The issue isn’t limited to the OS you mentioned, it can potentially affect any OS and it stems from a side effect applied to the response headers.

How I tested it
I disabled TTL generation so the cached response would always be returned.

What happens
The Gzip middleware, in addition to compressing the body, also adds or rewrites certain headers such as Content-Length and Content-Encoding.
This operation modifies those headers inside your cached response (a side effect).
On the next request (a cache hit), the headers are not recalculated because that only happens when the response is first created.
The response passes through the Gzip middleware again, but, based on the existing headers, the middleware forwards it directly, assuming it has already been compressed.
At that point an exception is raised because the declared length no longer matches the actual body.

Hope this helps =)

accepted_answer:
So, as I understand, this is what you needed:

```python
from collections.abc import Awaitable, Callable
from typing import Annotated, Optional

from fastapi import Depends, FastAPI, HTTPException, Request
from fastapi.security import HTTPBearer

class ValidateHTTPBearer(HTTPBearer):
    def __init__(
        self,
        *,
        scheme_name: Optional[str] = None,
        other_validations: list[Callable[[str], Awaitable[None]]],
    ):
        super().__init__(scheme_name=scheme_name)
        self._other_validations = other_validations

    async def validate_parse_token(self, token: str) -> dict:
        data = token.split(":")
        return {"user": data[0], "something": data[1]}

    async def validate_current_user(self, parsed_token: dict) -> str:
        return parsed_token["user"]

    async def __call__(self, request: Request) -> str:
        # Call the parent class to get the credentials
        auth_credentials = await super().__call__(request)

        # Validate the token and user
        parsed_token = await self.validate_parse_token(auth_credentials.credentials)
        user = await self.validate_current_user(parsed_token)

        # Perform other validations
        token_data = parsed_token.copy()
        token_data["user"] = user
        for validation in self._other_validations:
            await validation(token_data)

        return user


async def validate_token(token_data: dict):
    if token_data["something"] != "123":
        raise HTTPException(status_code=401, detail="Invalid token")

async def validate_user(token_data: dict):
    if token_data.get("user") != "admin":
        raise HTTPException(status_code=403, detail="Invalid user")

security = ValidateHTTPBearer(
    scheme_name="SomeBearer",
    other_validations=[validate_token, validate_user]
)

CurrentUser = Annotated[str, Depends(security)]

app = FastAPI()

@app.get("/")
def index(current_user: CurrentUser):
    return {"user": current_user}

```

And the answer to your question:

> Now I want to understand how is Async call being invoked and from where it is awaited?

FastAPI analyzes dependencies of the endpoint and calls\awaits them depending on the function signature.
Once you pass the instance of `ValidateHTTPBearer` as a dependency, it looks at the signature of `__call__` method and awaits it

accepted_answer:
Hi, since you're using an UploadFile, FastAPI/Starlette will interpret and store your post data as a multipart form. This is done internally via `await request.form()` as soon as the request is received. After that, the raw request data is no longer available and therefore can not be accessed via `await request.body()`.

Ironically, if the post data is first accessed via `await request.body()` it is possible to access it again via `await request.form()`, because the raw request data can be reinterpreted as multipart form data.

This leaves us with three options:

1. Option: work with form data in your `credential` dependency
    
    ```python
    async def credential(request: Request):
        form = await request.form()
    ```

2. Option: interpret the post data yourself

    ```python
    async def credential(request: Request):
        body = await request.body()  # No longer raises a runtime error
    
    
    @app.post("/api")
    async def read_root(
        request: Request,
        credential: Any = Depends(credential),
    ):
        form = await request.form()
        file = form.get("file")
        return {"Hello": file.filename if isinstance(file, UploadFile) else "no file"}
    ```

3. Option: start a discussion in the Starlette repo
    I'm pretty sure it's a performance optimization that the raw post data is no longer available if it has been accessed via `await request.form()` first. However, technically, it would be possible to preserve the raw post data in that case.

```python
Create a venv from the pex file:

One gets output like:

Encountered collision populating <dir>/example_venv from PEX at <dir>/example.pex:
1. <dir>/example_venv/bin/fastapi was provided by:
	sha1:e92b66b075fef87203d8ab355acfca9e7bbaac0f -> <pex_cache_path>/installed_wheels/0/c46ac7c312df840f0c9e220f7964bada936781bc4e2e6eb71f1c4d7553786565/fastapi-0.116.1-py3-none-any.whl/.prefix/bin/fastapi
	sha1:0829ef7f0cdb56ab1bac392120391d4a211e555b -> <pex_cache_path>/installed_wheels/0/0ea95d882c85b9219a75a65ab27e8da17dac02873e456850fa0a726e96e985eb/fastapi_cli-0.0.8-py3-none-any.whl/.prefix/bin/fastapi
```



### Description

My interaction with fastapi is only as a transitive dependency. My organization's build+deploy processes uses pex with venvs with an expanded and pinned set of transitive dependencies. In this context, I see an error due to `fastapi` and `fastapi_cli` wheels each exposing a `fastapi` script entrypoint: 
https://github.com/fastapi/fastapi/blob/master/pyproject.toml#L125
https://github.com/fastapi/fastapi-cli/blob/main/pyproject.toml#L57

However, the `fastapi`'s definition of the `fastapi` script entrypoint merely calls through to pathways in `fastapi_cli`. Since `fastapi_cli` also declares an entrypoint, we have two non-identical scripts registered with the same name. Upon manual inspection we can see that they should be equivalent but naturally build/env tools cannot establish this, and it's appropriate for them to warn over this collision.

It would be cleaner to remove one of the two definitions.

3.12.7

### Additional Context

Note, at present I think the double-declaration of this script / entrypoint causes unnecessary warnings or errors not only for direct users of fastapi, but also downstream projects who otherwise would have little reason to interact with fastapi.

WebSocket Chat

""" @app.get("/") async def get(): return HTMLResponse(html) # TODO FIXME scale horizontally @app.websocket("/ws") async def websocket_endpoint(websocket: WebSocket): await websocket.accept() while True: data = await websocket.receive_text() await websocket.send_text(f"Message text was: {data}") ``` ### Description * The docs link [encode/broadcaster](https://github.com/encode/broadcaster) which is now archived by owner and read-only. * Another recommendation from [Question 8684](https://github.com/fastapi/fastapi/discussions/8684), fastapi-socket.io is also now archived by owner and read-only. * Thus, I feel that the docs should be updated and am I looking for a recommendation with forward support. * What do people use and recommend? ### Operating System Linux ### Operating System Details _No response_ ### FastAPI Version Latest ### Pydantic Version 2.* ### Python Version 3.14 ### Additional Context _No response_
accepted_answer:
Since `broadcaster` and `fastapi-socketio` are archived, here are the actively maintained options in 2026:

## Recommended Solutions

### 1. **python-socketio** (Most Popular)
```bash
pip install python-socketio
```

```python
import socketio
from fastapi import FastAPI

sio = socketio.AsyncServer(async_mode='asgi', cors_allowed_origins='*')
app = FastAPI()
socket_app = socketio.ASGIApp(sio, app)

@sio.event
async def connect(sid, environ):
    print(f"Client connected: {sid}")

@sio.event
async def message(sid, data):
    await sio.emit('response', {'data': data}, room=sid)
```

For horizontal scaling, use Redis adapter:
```python
import socketio

mgr = socketio.AsyncRedisManager('redis://localhost:6379')
sio = socketio.AsyncServer(client_manager=mgr, async_mode='asgi')
```

### 2. **Redis Pub/Sub Directly** (Simplest)
```python
import redis.asyncio as redis
from fastapi import WebSocket

redis_client = redis.from_url("redis://localhost:6379")

@app.websocket("/ws/{channel}")
async def websocket_endpoint(websocket: WebSocket, channel: str):
    await websocket.accept()
    pubsub = redis_client.pubsub()
    await pubsub.subscribe(channel)

    async for message in pubsub.listen():
        if message["type"] == "message":
            await websocket.send_text(message["data"].decode())
```

### 3. **Centrifugo** (Production-Grade)
Standalone server, connects via HTTP API:
- Handles millions of connections
- Built-in Redis/NATS/Kafka support
- Dashboard included

GitHub: https://github.com/centrifugal/centrifugo

### Comparison

| Solution | Complexity | Scalability | Maintenance |
|----------|------------|-------------|-------------|
| python-socketio + Redis | Medium | High | Active |
| Redis Pub/Sub | Low | High | N/A (Redis) |
| Centrifugo | High (setup) | Very High | Active |

**My recommendation**: Start with `python-socketio` + Redis adapter. It's the most documented and actively maintained option for FastAPI in 2026.

title: Should commercial deploy tooling ship by default in the `[standard]` extra?
question_body:
Hi Sebastián and team,

I want to raise an ergonomic / supply-chain-hygiene question about a change in fastapi `0.136.3`, *not* as a complaint about the underlying choice but as feedback on how it lands for downstream maintainers and security tooling. I'm a fastapi user shipping a framework that depends on fastapi transitively.

### Context

In `0.136.3`, the `[standard]` extras group gained two transitive deps via `fastapi-cli[standard]` → `fastapi-cloud-cli`:

- `fastar>=0.9.0` — Rust tar bindings, used by `fastapi-cloud-cli/commands/deploy.py:127` to write zstd-compressed tarballs for cloud upload. Completely legitimate; the name is `fast`+`tar`.
- `sentry-sdk`, `rignore`, etc. — telemetry + Rust-backed gitignore parsing for the deploy flow.

`pyproject.toml` cleanly declares both `standard` and the new `standard-no-fastapi-cloud-cli` extras — so opt-out exists for users who want it, which I appreciate.

### What's happened downstream

The Amazon Inspector vulnerability database has issued advisory `MAL-2026-4750` flagging `0.136.3` as a malicious release. The advisory's substantive claims are wrong (`fastar` is not a typosquat, the dep has a legitimate purpose, the opt-out extra demonstrates intentional design), but pip-audit + similar tooling propagate the finding to every project that resolves `fastapi==0.136.3`. As of writing, every downstream project running `pip-audit --strict` in CI is red-blocked. The advisory will probably be retracted eventually, but in the meantime maintainers across the ecosystem are pinning `!=0.136.3` defensively.

That's not your responsibility to fix and I don't think you owe anyone a response to it. But it surfaces a real ergonomic question that I think *is* worth a conversation:

### The actual question

The canonical install doc still says `pip install "fastapi[standard]"`. With `0.136.3`, this:

1. Adds commercial-deploy tooling (`fastapi-cloud-cli` → FastAPI Cloud) to the default-recommended install path.
2. Pulls in Rust-backed deps with single-maintainer authorship (`fastar`, `rignore`).
3. Adds outbound-network telemetry (`sentry-sdk`).

The opt-out extra (`standard-no-fastapi-cloud-cli`) exists, which is great — but it requires users to (a) know the cloud-cli is now bundled, (b) know they don't want it, and (c) remember to type a much longer extras name. Most users following the official docs will install the full `[standard]`.

**Would the team consider one of these?**

- **(A)** Promote `standard-no-fastapi-cloud-cli` (perhaps under a shorter name like `serve` or `core-standard`) to be the *primary* recommended install, with `[standard]` opt-in for cloud-cli users.
- **(B)** Leave the resolution as-is but add a clearer call-out in the `[standard]` install docs that it now bundles commercial deploy tooling, with a one-liner pointer to the opt-out extra.
- **(C)** Move `fastar` and the other cloud-cli-specific transitive deps so they're declared in `fastapi-cloud-cli`'s own `[standard]` (which they are, currently) but *not* re-declared in fastapi's `[standard]` — i.e. let users get them only when they install `fastapi-cli[standard]` explicitly. (This may already be the structure; I haven't fully traced it.)

None of these is urgent. The current shape is defensible — I'm only flagging the question because a lot of downstream maintainers got a confusing CI red today, and the trajectory of "framework's recommended install path silently grows commercial tooling" is worth a moment of explicit thought even if the outcome is "yes, that's the trade-off we're making."

Thanks for fastapi. Happy to provide more context on the pip-audit failure path if useful.
accepted_answer:
Thanks for the comment!

About the false positive from Amazon, more of the context is here: https://github.com/ossf/malicious-packages/issues/1274 , it seems it was an automated AI scan that reported a vulnerability, got accepted, created a CVE, etc. without ever even attempting to contact us. :smiling_face_with_tear:  But they are withdrawing it now.

About single-maintainer dependencies, that's how most of the entire open source ecosystem works, in most cases works fine, and in most cases there's one specific person (or a very small few) leading a project, that's not really an issue. The fact that it's under a person's username also doesn't limit permissions to maintain, they could add extra people. Same with an org, the fact that it's an org doesn't necessarily change things, it could still be a single person leading.

About the default `standard` dependencies, your option C is what already is in place, sadly, the automated detection didn't even check that.

About how to explain what is installed and done, we do that profusely, it's in the docs, sadly there's no easy way to explain more than that. We don't have a direct channel with users, not even telemetry. Sentry is installed for the cloud CLI for when there are errors deploying, but that's not activated when running the regular FastAPI commands. It would be very useful to know what things people use and what not, to be able to deprecate things, but we don't do that as that would raise concerns, it's only for cloud users.

The current decision to make those things part of `standard` is that that is the standard experience I would think users could get by default:

* It is designed to be the default, official, and simplest way to deploy FastAPI to the cloud. Anyone can deploy it to any other platform, but that is the one made by and for FastAPI.
* The default is made to be the one with the lowest friction, if a user needs to perform a bunch of additional steps just to get the recommended experience of deploying, then it's not as straightforward as it should it, which is also the spirit of FastAPI in general, to have good defaults on. Important in particular to newcomers to FastAPI and Python.
* It is already opt-in, people have to install `"fastapi[standard]"` to get that plus the other things (e.g. uvloop and httptools for high performance). But if they simply install `fastapi`, they won't get any of that.
* FastAPI Cloud is also our way of sustainability for the open source projects, and it's quite aligned with them, as the more effectively people can use Python and the open source tools, more potential clients down the line for the company, so it's aligned even if it was independent of me.

## What needs attention and fixing: automated AI reports

Now, I want to raise an important issue that is not discussed in the original post, that should probably get attention, and I don't know the right way to solve it.

AI automated tools from organizations with access to create CVEs directly should not go and create them based on an AI hunch. 

First, these things should be responsibly disclosed to the projects, in private, allowing handling of the vulnerability properly, not reporting via a third party, and then us getting to know about a "vulnerability in FastAPI" via users complaining. That's quite wrong.

Second, if they flag something, that should be reviewed by human researchers before reporting.

Third, the combination of giving some AI authorization to automatically create CVEs seems quite dangerous to me. That should definitely have a human review.

I use AI a lot, I appreciate how much it helps, but that's the wrong way to use it.

Anyway, I don't have a way to solve that, I don't expect you would, but I wanted to highlight an important factor in this situation that causes a lot of friction and I don't think should simply go unnoticed.

title: app.frontend() with fallback="index.html" returns 404 for client side routes that have a dot in the last path segment (like /users/john.doe or /v/1.2.3)
question_body:
### First Check

- [x] I added a very descriptive title here.
- [x] I used the GitHub search to find a similar question and didn't find it.
- [x] I searched the FastAPI documentation, with the integrated search.
- [x] I already searched in Google "How to X in FastAPI" and didn't find any information.

- [x] I already checked if it is not related to FastAPI but to Pydantic.
- [x] I already checked if it is not related to FastAPI but to Swagger UI.
- [x] I already checked if it is not related to FastAPI but to ReDoc.

### Commit to Help

- [x] I commit to help with one of those options 👆

### Example Code

```python
import os
import tempfile

from fastapi import FastAPI
from fastapi.testclient import TestClient

dist = tempfile.mkdtemp()
with open(os.path.join(dist, "index.html"), "w") as f:
    f.write("<html>SPA shell</html>")

app = FastAPI()
app.frontend("/", directory=dist, fallback="index.html")

client = TestClient(app)

# The Accept header a browser sends on a normal top level navigation.
browser_nav = {
    "accept": "text/html,application/xhtml+xml,application/xml;q=0.9,"
    "image/avif,image/webp,image/apng,*/*;q=0.8"
}

print(client.get("/users/john", headers=browser_nav).status_code)      # 200, serves index.html
print(client.get("/users/john.doe", headers=browser_nav).status_code)  # 404
print(client.get("/v/1.2.3", headers=browser_nav).status_code)         # 404
```

### Description

Hi 👋

I have been trying out the new `app.frontend()` helper to serve a single page app, using `fallback="index.html"` so that client side routes fall back to the shell and the frontend router can take over. This is the behavior described in the "Client side routing" part of the docs, and it works fine for a path like `/dashboard` or `/dashboard/settings`.

The problem shows up when a client side route has a dot in its last path segment. Plenty of real apps have these, for example a profile at `/users/john.doe`, a version deep link at `/v/1.2.3`, or a slug like `/files/report.2024`. When I open one of those directly, or just hit refresh while I am already on that page, I get a 404 instead of the `index.html` shell, so the app never loads and the client router never gets a chance to handle the route.

The part that surprised me is that setting `fallback="index.html"` explicitly does not change this. As far as I can tell there is currently no way to get these routes to fall back to the shell.

I spent some time reading the code and I think it comes from `_is_frontend_navigation_request()` in `fastapi/routing.py`. It takes the last path segment and if `os.path.splitext(...)` finds an extension it returns early and treats the request as an asset request, before it ever looks at the `Accept` header. Because `os.path.splitext("john.doe")` returns `.doe`, any segment with a dot in it is treated as a file and never gets the `index.html` fallback, even when the browser clearly asked for `text/html`.

What makes me think this is fixable without regressions is that the two situations are easy to tell apart. A real browser navigation sends `Accept: text/html`, while a missing asset requested from a script tag, an image tag, or a fetch call sends `*/*` or a specific type like `text/css`. If I request a genuinely missing asset such as `/assets/missing.js` with `Accept: */*` it still returns 404 as expected, so checking the `Accept` header first would fix the navigation case and keep the asset case working.

I did notice there is already a test that pins the current behavior. `test_index_fallback_does_not_handle_asset_like_or_non_html_requests` has a `("/users/jane.doe", "text/html")` case that expects a 404, so before proposing a change I wanted to ask whether the current behavior is intentional. If the idea is that dotted client routes should be servable, would a change that treats an explicit `Accept: text/html` request as navigation regardless of the path be acceptable? Or would you rather keep the extension heuristic as the default for `fallback="auto"` and add an opt in for apps that use dotted client side routes?

I am happy to open a PR with a failing test and the change for whichever direction you prefer. Thanks a lot for the work on this feature.

### Operating System

Windows

### Operating System Details

Also reproduced on current master. The logic involved is pure routing code, so it is not tied to any particular operating system.

### FastAPI Version

0.139.0

### Pydantic Version

2.13.4

### Python Version

3.11

### Additional Context

_No response_

Indeed, this should be fixed. I'm tracking it here in this issue for completeness: https://github.com/fastapi/fastapi/issues/16010 , and fix PR here: https://github.com/fastapi/fastapi/pull/16011

title: Behavioral difference between standard `with`  and `contextmanager_in_threadpool`
question_body:
### First Check

- [X] I added a very descriptive title here.
- [X] I used the GitHub search to find a similar question and didn't find it.
- [X] I searched the FastAPI documentation, with the integrated search.
- [X] I already searched in Google "How to X in FastAPI" and didn't find any information.
- [X] I already read and followed all the tutorial in the docs and didn't find an answer.
- [X] I already checked if it is not related to FastAPI but to [Pydantic](https://github.com/pydantic/pydantic).
- [X] I already checked if it is not related to FastAPI but to [Swagger UI](https://github.com/swagger-api/swagger-ui).
- [X] I already checked if it is not related to FastAPI but to [ReDoc](https://github.com/Redocly/redoc).

### Commit to Help

- [X] I commit to help with one of those options 👆

### Example Code

```python
import asyncio
from fastapi.concurrency import contextmanager_in_threadpool


class TrackingCM:
    """Context manager that tracks whether __exit__ is called."""
    
    def __init__(self, name: str):
        self.name = name
        self.exit_called = False
    
    def __enter__(self):
        print(f"  [{self.name}] __enter__ called")
        raise ValueError("setup failed")
    
    def __exit__(self, exc_type, exc_val, exc_tb):
        self.exit_called = True
        print(f"  [{self.name}] __exit__ called  <-- PEP 343 violation!")


async def main():
    print("=" * 70)
    print("Behavioral inconsistency with Python context manager protocol")
    print("=" * 70)
    
    print("\n1. Standard Python `with`:")
    cm1 = TrackingCM("standard")
    try:
        with cm1:
            pass
    except ValueError:
        pass
    print(f"   Result: exit_called = {cm1.exit_called}")
    print(f"   OK: __exit__ NOT called when __enter__ raises")
    
    print("\n2. contextmanager_in_threadpool:")
    cm2 = TrackingCM("threadpool")
    try:
        async with contextmanager_in_threadpool(cm2):
            pass
    except ValueError:
        pass
    print(f"   Result: exit_called = {cm2.exit_called}")
    if cm2.exit_called:
        print(f"   FAIL: __exit__ IS called when __enter__ raises")
    
    print("\n" + "=" * 70)
    print("Root cause:")
    print("=" * 70)
    print("In fastapi/concurrency.py:")
    print("  try:")
    print("      yield await run_in_threadpool(cm.__enter__)  # if raises -> except")
    print("  except Exception as e:")
    print("      ok = bool(await anyio.to_thread.run_sync(cm.__exit__, ...))")
    print("")
    print("When __enter__ raises, the exception falls into `except`, and __exit__")
    print("is called. In standard Python `with`, if __enter__ raises, __exit__ is")
    print("NOT called (the context was never entered).")
    print("=" * 70)


if __name__ == "__main__":
    asyncio.run(main())
```


### Description

I`m wrapping a sync context manager with contextmanager_in_threadpool. When __enter__ raises, I expect __exit__ to NOT be called, per PEP 343 (the context was never entered). Instead, __exit__ IS called. See the Minimal Reproducible Example (MRE).

### Operating System

Linux

### Operating System Details

Ubuntu 24.04 LTS

### FastAPI Version

0.139.0

### Pydantic Version

2.13.4

### Python Version

3.11.14

### Additional Context

_No response_
accepted_answer:
Thanks for confirming this Sergei @yudin-s, and for the fix. Moving `__enter__` out of the `try` fixes the first issue cleanly (and it also stops `__exit__` swallowing the `__enter__` exception when it returned `True`, which the old `except` block used to do).

I kept digging and found two more deviations from PEP 343 that the fix alone does not cover.

**2. `except Exception` skips `BaseException`**

The guard catches `Exception` but not `BaseException`. So `KeyboardInterrupt`, `SystemExit`, and `asyncio.CancelledError` raised in the body never reach `__exit__`. A standard `with` calls `__exit__` for all of these:

```python
class T:
    def __enter__(self): return self
    def __exit__(self, *a):
        print("exit called", a[0])
        return False

try:
    with T():
        raise KeyboardInterrupt()
except KeyboardInterrupt:
    pass
# standard with: exit runs, receives KeyboardInterrupt
# contextmanager_in_threadpool: exit never runs
```

So the guard needs to be `except BaseException`.

**3. Real anyio cancellation never reaches `__exit__`**

This one is sneakier. Even with `except BaseException`, a real task cancellation (via `cancel_scope.cancel()`) still does not run `__exit__`. The `await anyio.to_thread.run_sync(...)` call is itself a checkpoint: anyio sees the scope is still cancelled and re-raises `CancelledError` before the worker thread starts.

I confirmed this by canceling a task group child parked inside the context:

```python
async with anyio.create_task_group() as tg:
    async def child():
        async with contextmanager_in_threadpool(cm):
            await anyio.sleep(10)
    tg.start_soon(child)
    await anyio.sleep(0.1)
    tg.cancel_scope.cancel()
# cm.exit_called == False
```

That is the worst case for cleanup: cancellation is exactly when you want `__exit__` to run, and it is exactly when it gets skipped.

**4. The else (normal exit) branch has the same hole**

The `else` branch runs `__exit__(None, None, None)` after a body that completed without raising. Its `await anyio.to_thread.run_sync(...)` is a checkpoint too. If a cancel lands in the window between a checkpoint-free body returning and that await, `__exit__` is skipped while `__enter__` already ran - a straight resource leak. Reproducible:

```python
async with anyio.create_task_group() as tg:
    async def child():
        async with contextmanager_in_threadpool(cm):
            entered.set()   # body has no other await
    tg.start_soon(child)
    await entered.wait()
    tg.cancel_scope.cancel()
# without a shield on the else branch: cm.exit_called == False
# enter ran, exit did not
```

That window is narrow, but it is real. For a cleanup callback it should not exist at all.

**Fix: shield every `__exit__` thread call**

```python
exit_limiter = CapacityLimiter(1)
value = await run_in_threadpool(cm.__enter__)
try:
    yield value
except BaseException as e:
    with anyio.CancelScope(shield=True):
        ok = bool(
            await anyio.to_thread.run_sync(
                cm.__exit__, type(e), e, e.__traceback__, limiter=exit_limiter
            )
        )
    if not ok:
        raise
else:
    with anyio.CancelScope(shield=True):
        await anyio.to_thread.run_sync(
            cm.__exit__, None, None, None, limiter=exit_limiter
        )
```

Both `__exit__` calls are now shielded. The mental model is simple: once `__enter__` has run, `__exit__` always runs to completion, cancellation or not. This mirrors what a synchronous `with` already does: `__exit__` is a sync call, you cannot cancel it mid-flight.

Here are the tests that pin each of the cases above, so it is not just a claim. All run on both asyncio and trio (`@pytest.mark.anyio`), so the asyncio and trio variants are separate test items.

```python
class EnterFailsCM:
    def __init__(self, exit_return: bool | None = False) -> None:
        self.exit_called = False
        self.exit_return = exit_return

    def __enter__(self) -> str:
        raise ValueError("setup failed")

    def __exit__(self, exc_type, exc_val, exc_tb) -> bool | None:
        self.exit_called = True
        return self.exit_return


@pytest.mark.anyio
async def test_enter_failure_does_not_call_exit() -> None:
    cm = EnterFailsCM()
    with pytest.raises(ValueError, match="setup failed"):
        async with contextmanager_in_threadpool(cm):
            pass
    assert not cm.exit_called


@pytest.mark.anyio
async def test_enter_failure_propagates_even_if_exit_would_suppress() -> None:
    # old code: __exit__(True) would swallow the __enter__ ValueError
    cm = EnterFailsCM(exit_return=True)
    with pytest.raises(ValueError, match="setup failed"):
        async with contextmanager_in_threadpool(cm):
            pass
    assert not cm.exit_called


class ExitTrackingCM:
    def __init__(self) -> None:
        self.exit_called = False
        self.exit_args: tuple = ()

    def __enter__(self) -> str:
        return "value"

    def __exit__(self, exc_type, exc_val, exc_tb) -> bool:
        self.exit_called = True
        self.exit_args = (exc_type, exc_val, exc_tb)
        return False


@pytest.mark.anyio
async def test_keyboard_interrupt_in_body_calls_exit() -> None:
    cm = ExitTrackingCM()
    with pytest.raises(KeyboardInterrupt, match="boom"):
        async with contextmanager_in_threadpool(cm):
            raise KeyboardInterrupt("boom")
    assert cm.exit_called
    assert cm.exit_args[0] is KeyboardInterrupt


# SystemExit and manual asyncio.CancelledError are covered by two more tests
# of the same shape (test_system_exit_in_body_calls_exit,
# test_cancelled_error_in_body_calls_exit).


class SlowExitTrackingCM:
    def __init__(self) -> None:
        self.exit_called = False

    def __enter__(self) -> str:
        return "value"

    def __exit__(self, exc_type, exc_val, exc_tb) -> bool:
        self.exit_called = True
        return False


@pytest.mark.anyio
async def test_real_cancellation_still_calls_exit() -> None:
    import anyio

    cm = SlowExitTrackingCM()

    async with anyio.create_task_group() as tg:
        async def child() -> None:
            async with contextmanager_in_threadpool(cm):
                await anyio.sleep(10)

        tg.start_soon(child)
        await anyio.sleep(0.1)
        tg.cancel_scope.cancel()

    assert cm.exit_called


@pytest.mark.anyio
async def test_cancellation_after_normal_body_still_calls_exit() -> None:
    import anyio

    cm = SlowExitTrackingCM()
    entered = anyio.Event()

    async with anyio.create_task_group() as tg:
        async def child() -> None:
            async with contextmanager_in_threadpool(cm):
                entered.set()

        tg.start_soon(child)
        await entered.wait()
        tg.cancel_scope.cancel()

    assert cm.exit_called
```

The last test is the one that made me add the shield on the else branch too: without it, `assert cm.exit_called` fails on the asyncio backend (enter ran, exit did not). With the shield, it passes on both backends.

I have a full set of tests covering these cases locally. An earlier version went up as a PR but got closed/rejected, so I reworked it: the enter-out-of-try, the `BaseException` guard, and the shields on both branches are all pinned by tests now, on both asyncio and trio.

One tradeoff to flag: if `__exit__` blocks (rollback to a dead DB), cancellation cannot interrupt it until `__exit__` returns. That is the same constraint as a plain `with`, but it is worth being explicit about it.

title: [0.118.0] Use case for early closing in yield dependencies (session commit before response)
question_body:
### First Check

- [X] I added a very descriptive title here.
